detail.abstract: Perishable exports such as fresh fruit, vegetables, flowers, seafood, and meat lose value every hour they spend out of their ideal temperature range. Between harvest and retail, about 14 percent of the world's food is lost, and the lack of effective refrigeration alone is estimated to cost 526 million tonnes of food production a year. For exporters, loss appears as rejected consignments, discounted sales, and damaged reputations. This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can turn cold chain data into decisions, and how agentic AI, systems that pursue a goal through multistep workflows using software tools, can act on those decisions across farms, packhouses, carriers, and buyers. It reviews the case for intelligent logistics that replaces fixed dates with measured remaining shelf life and allocates stock by first-expired-first-out rather than first-in-first-out. It proposes a five-stage framework spanning harvest, packhouse, transport, port and customs, and destination, and illustrates an agentic temperature-excursion workflow that assesses shelf-life impact, re-plans the consignment, and escalates costly decisions to a manager. It argues that the largest gains come from acting on cold chain data in time, not only collecting it, and it closes with a key performance indicator (KPI) set for loss, quality, cost, and governance.

detail.abstract: For perishable exports, a missing signature or a mismatched weight on a certificate can cost more than a temperature excursion: the consignment waits at the border while its shelf life runs out. Exporters must satisfy a web of requirements that differ by product and destination, including phytosanitary certificates, health certificates, certificates of origin, residue limits, labeling rules, and customs declarations. This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can reduce compliance errors and delays, and how agentic AI, systems that pursue a goal through multistep workflows using software tools, can assemble and check an export document set end to end. It reviews the shift to electronic certification, including 96 countries digitalizing phytosanitary certification through the international ePhyto Solution, and the trade facilitation commitments that encourage paperless trade. It proposes a five-stage framework spanning market requirements, production records, document preparation, submission, and clearance, and illustrates an agentic document workflow in which a regulatory gate routes any novel or ambiguous requirement to a licensed customs broker or compliance officer. It argues that AI helps most by catching inconsistencies before goods move, and it closes with a key performance indicator (KPI) set for clearance time, rejection rate, and governance.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used in digital forensics to help investigators work through large volumes of data, identify patterns, detect anomalies, and reduce repetitive analysis. These capabilities can speed up forensic work and improve efficiency. They also raise an important question: how can an AI-assisted finding be trusted and defended when it becomes part of an investigation or legal proceeding?

Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods such as SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) can help investigators understand which features influenced an AI model's output. The value of that explanation depends on the model's reliability, the explanation's quality, and the forensic process surrounding its use. This white paper reviews recent research on XAI in digital forensics alongside selected NIST and ISO guidance on AI governance and digital evidence handling. The review identifies several factors that contribute to forensic defensibility, including model validation, explanation fidelity and stability, evidence integrity and provenance, repeatability, documentation, human oversight, and governance. Based on these findings, the paper presents an AI-Forensic Defensibility Model to assess AI-assisted forensic findings and place XAI within a controlled forensic process.

detail.abstract: Perishable exporters make a chain of commercial decisions under severe time pressure: how much to plant and harvest, which markets to sell to, which lots to send where, and whether to ship by air or by sea. Each decision must be made before demand is known and before the product's remaining shelf life is certain, and mistakes turn into discounted sales, spoiled stock, or unmet contracts. This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can improve these decisions and how agentic AI, systems that pursue a goal through multistep workflows using software tools, can coordinate them across growers, packhouses, carriers, and buyers. It reviews evidence from large forecasting competitions that machine learning methods can improve demand forecasts, and the case for allocating perishables by measured shelf life rather than fixed dates. It proposes a five-stage planning framework spanning season planning, market selection, lot allocation, mode and route choice, and sales execution, and illustrates an agentic weekly allocation workflow in which a margin gate routes commercially significant changes to a sales manager. It argues that AI's value in perishable trade lies in matching supply to demand while the product is still fresh, and it closes with a key performance indicator (KPI) set for margin, loss, service, and governance.

detail.abstract: This project compares three distinct positions in the AI economy: JPMorgan Chase as the primary representative of the financial industry, Berkshire Hathaway as a diversified and asset-heavy XLF holding, and NVIDIA as the leading AI-infrastructure producer in XLK. JPMorgan is the better financial-sector benchmark because its earnings, assets, regulation, technology spending, and AI applications arise directly from banking, payments, markets, lending, fraud control, and wealth management. Berkshire remains useful as a contrast, but its insurance operations are combined with rail, utilities, energy, manufacturing, service, and retail businesses, so consolidated capital expenditure is not a clean measure of financial-industry technology adoption. The analysis therefore uses JPMorgan to assess bank-specific AI efficiency, Berkshire to illustrate diversified and less observable adoption, and NVIDIA to illustrate direct AI monetization. Main finding. JPMorgan provides the most economically relevant financial-industry comparison with NVIDIA. The bank deploys AI inside regulated, data-intensive workflows-including fraud detection, credit, trading, payments, customer service, software development, and wealth advice-while maintaining a large technology budget and a balance sheet shaped by loans, deposits, liquidity, and regulatory capital. Its AI payoff should therefore be evaluated through productivity, expense efficiency, revenue quality, risk outcomes, return on equity, and return on tangible common equity, not through industrial capex ratios alone. JPMorgan s 2025 annual report records $57.0 billion of net income, $4.4 trillion of assets, 17% ROE, and 20% ROTCE, while management describes AI as part of a broad technology and operating transformation. Berkshire still shows a shallow, difficult-to-observe J-curve, and NVIDIA shows the clearest post-investment

detail.title: The Strengthened 2022 Code of Practice on Disinformation: Continuities and Innovations in EU Digital Regulation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

affiliations.org_name: University of Malta - Department of Law

detail.abstract:
This article examines the evolution of the European Union's regulatory framework addressing digital disinformation, tracing the trajectory from early safe-harbor models of intermediary liability to the structured, risk-based co-regulation established under the Digital Services Act (DSA). From the vantage point of EU IT law, the central difficulty lies in balancing fundamental rights with the urgent need to mitigate the severe societal harms caused by informational distortions. To contextualise the legal design, the analysis establishes a conceptual taxonomy distinguishing between unintentional misinformation, intentional disinformation, and coordinated influence operations. These distinctions do not serve mere academic dogma; they bear directly on legal design and the calibration of proportionate regulatory interventions. 

The paper analyses how the Strengthened 2022 Code of Practice on Disinformation translates the DSA's open-textured systemic-risk obligations into actionable commitments for Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPS) and Search Engines (VLOSES).

title: Digital Banking, Deposit Rents, and Fragility
affiliations: University of Navarra

detail.title: Digital Banking, Deposit Rents, and Fragility
detail.abstract: Digitalization improves banks’ monitoring of distant projects. When does it nonetheless make banks riskier? In a spatial model of deposit competition, digitalization also lowers transportation costs and erodes the market power banks earn from proximity. Under a flat deposit insurance premium, monitoring incentives are proportional to deposit rents, and in locations where banks compete directly for every depositor the loss of rents outweighs the monitoring gain, raising aggregate fragility. In local monopoly regions, digitalization stabilizes banks beyond a threshold distance that increases with the cost of remote interaction. Under fair premiums, monitoring no longer depends on rents and digitalization lowers aggregate fragility.

title: Task-Technology Fit and Communication Synchronicity as Drivers of Microsoft Teams Collaboration Effectiveness: Evidence from Users in Bangladesh
affiliations: Shanto-Mariam University of Creative Technology and Shanto-Mariam University of Creative Technology

detail.title: Task-Technology Fit and Communication Synchronicity as Drivers of Microsoft Teams Collaboration Effectiveness: Evidence from Users in Bangladesh

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study used a non-interventional, minimal-risk questionnaire survey of adult participants. Participation was voluntary, the purpose of the study was communicated to respondents, and informed consent was obtained before participation. No direct personal identifiers were collected in the analytical dataset. At the time the research was conducted, the authors’ university did not require formal institutional ethics-committee approval for this category of non-clinical, non-interventional academic survey; therefore, no formal ethics approval number was issued.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Digital collaboration platforms combine task-support functionality with synchronous and asynchronous communication, yet these mechanisms are often examined separately. This study investigates whether task-technology fit (TTF) and communication synchronicity (CS) independently explain perceived Microsoft Teams collaboration effectiveness (CE), and whether CS strengthens the TTF-CE relationship. A cross-sectional survey dataset comprising 385 complete responses from Microsoft-platform users in Bangladesh was analysed. Data auditing confirmed complete focal responses, no duplicate respondent identifiers, valid 1-5 response coding, and no evidence of reverse-coded or miscoded focal items. Reliability was modest (Cronbach's α: TTF=.565, CS=.526, CE=.515), reflecting weak-to-moderate inter-item correlations rather than a single coding anomaly; deleting any one item did not materially resolve the problem. Composite-based diagnostics were more favorable (CR=.775/.760/.756; AVE=.535/.514/.509), while HTMT values remained below .85. Standardized composite-score regression showed positive associations of TTF (β=.257, p<.001) and CS (β=.211, p<.001) with CE, explaining 15.6% of its variance. The TTF×CS interaction was not significant (β=.016, p=.716). The findings support a parallel-mechanism interpretation: perceived task fit and communication-process support each matter for collaboration, but synchronicity does not amplify the contribution of task fit in this sample. The study contributes a boundary-condition test integrating Task-Technology Fit and Media Synchronicity Theory while explicitly recognizing measurement and cross-sectional limitations.

detail.abstract: The Kubernetes Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) configurations decrease in quality as time passes. The current paper includes a longitudinal overview of the RBAC drift in clusters of production over a 6-to 12 months duration that unexpectedly discusses the differences in role assignments and their initial planning as access policies. Based on quantitative drift measures, organization control audit data and field observations, the researcher determines what drives the most in accumulating of permission and builds a mathematics to measure the drift velocity. Findings indicate that clusters deployed in organizations that have weak governance structures have statistically-significant permission bloat within half a year after their deployment. The rate of drift is highly moderated by organizational aspects of the group size, the frequency of release and the frequency of audit. The results support policy reconciliation tooling based on automation and the organized review of the permission as the most effective countermeasures.

detail.abstract: From 12 January 2027, switching cloud provider will cost nothing. In France, this has already been the case since a ministerial order of 17 November 2025. What remains to be seen is what you take with you. Contracts promise a "reasonable and common format", that is to say, tables. What does not leave is the model: the functional hierarchy, the classifications, the rules. And the regulation that organises the exit excludes it in its very definition. This study reads Chapter VI of the EU Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854) against the French SREN Act, the exit clauses of IBM's cloud terms, the answers of three asset management system suppliers to the same UK G-Cloud questions, a 2004 NIST cost study, the Birmingham City Council ERP case and Ofwat's 2024 asset health roadmap, and proposes five procurement requirements anchored on ISO 55001:2024 clause 7.6, IEC 81346 and ISO 14224. This paper is the English version, translated by the author, of Cahiers de technopolitique no. 3 (French original DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22836960). title: Refusal Bites only up to Spare Cash: Who Must Hold the Budget When Public Services Turn Harmful
affiliations: The University of Danang

detail.title: Refusal Bites only up to Spare Cash: Who Must Hold the Budget When Public Services Turn Harmful

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests: no financial or personal relationship with any person or organization that could influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. It was funded by the author.

detail.abstract: A right to refuse harmful terms is worth only what the buyer can afford. We study a deployed public service whose agency ignores a harm borne by residents, and ask who should hold two rights: financing an alternative, and refusing the incumbent's offer. A refusal right makes the supplier pay for the harm only up to the buyer's spare cash, the priced slack. A better alternative can increase that slack; spending can reduce it. Theorem 1 gives a characterisation, over the stated no-legacy, zero-overhead domain of the model, of when residents must hold both rights. There are three cases. Residents build an alternative and switch to it (fallback). They build one, never use it, and the incumbent serves without the harm (threat). Or they keep cash unspent, because an agency holding the budget would spend it and so disable their refusal (drain). Theorem 2 shows that residents weakly prefer joint rights throughout the baseline model. Proposition 1 shows that cheaper harmful service can stop protective investment while weakly raising resident welfare and total surplus. The results assume enforceable resident representation and an operable alternative. Documentary cases show what must be measured to apply the model and do not test it.

title: Collective Superintelligence – Keeping Humans in the AI Loop
affiliations: Unanimous AI

detail.title: Collective Superintelligence – Keeping Humans in the AI Loop

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Louis Rosenberg is employed by Unanimous AI
declarations.funderStatement: Some of the research cited was funded in part by National Science Foundation and the US Air Force

detail.abstract: Aligning AI systems with human values, interests, and sensibilities remains an unsolved problem that poses growing societal risks as organizations integrate AI models into decision-making processes. To address these risks, this chapter advocates for Collective Superintelligence (CSI), a hybrid paradigm in which human stakeholders and AI agents form real-time deliberative systems inspired by the decision-making dynamics of fish schools, bird flocks, and other natural collectives. The objective is to enable massively scalable hybrid teams of humans and AI agents to collaboratively solve complex problems more effectively than any individual members (human or AI), while ensuring that human values, goals, and interests remain integral to the process. Specifically, this chapter reviews a novel hyper-communication framework called Conversational Swarm Intelligence (Hyperchat) and describes how it overcomes the limitations of traditional collective intelligence methods. Empirical studies demonstrate that this framework has promise for enabling large-scale human-AI systems to solve problems with significantly amplified intelligence while ensuring that human perspectives remain central to the decision-making loop. Ultimately, CSI may offer a scalable path to an aligned superintelligence that elevates human wisdom, agency, and interests rather than replacing them.

title: Structural Capital Intelligence: From Probabilistic Intelligence to Deterministic Institutional Execution - A Framework for Identifying Durable Value and the Reallocation of Enterprise AI Economics

detail.abstract:
The current artificial intelligence market is heavily concentrated around frontier model providers whose valuations assume that probabilistic intelligence will remain a primary economic value layer of enterprise AI. This paper proposes a structural counter-thesis: as enterprise AI matures toward consequential action, durable economic value may increasingly shift away from raw probabilistic inference toward the institutional and execution layers that govern authorization, state transitions, provenance, and policy enforcement.

Large language models (LLMs) and generative neural networks are fundamentally stochastic architectures and do not provide deterministic institutional guarantees at the model layer alone. Instead, this paper proposes that enterprise AI is evolving toward an architectural separation: probabilistic intelligence generates proposals, while deterministic execution infrastructure controls whether those proposals become authorized, auditable institutional state changes.

Using Structural Capital Intelligence (SCI) as an analytical framework, this paper examines how value may migrate from model-layer API consumption toward constrained automation and agent-governance layers. It further examines how this transition could create a duration mismatch for model providers operating under large, non-cancelable compute obligations. The paper proposes the Capacity Coverage Ratio (CCR) as a discounted, probability-adjusted underwriting framework for comparing scenario-based contribution cash flows with binding infrastructure obligations over a stated measurement horizon. Applying the framework to reported 2026 enterprise AI infrastructure data, including Anthropic's reported infrastructure commitments, the paper formulates falsifiable conditions under which economic value reallocation across the enterprise AI stack would be observable.

detail.abstract: Digital platforms shape the preferences of the users they serve. Governance and curation decide what users encounter, and repeated encounters change what users value. Research in computer science, economics, and communication has shown that such shaping occurs and that it feeds back into platform decisions, but platform theory has paid less attention to who captures the demand a platform makes. We distinguish a platform-specific component of induced preference change, attached to complements, relationships, and skills that exist only on the shaping platform, from a portable component, attached to formats and categories that rivals can also offer. When users multi-home and rivals can imitate the format, they can harvest the portable component. A minimal two-platform model gives a closed-form condition under which a platform's shaping raises a rival's demand more than its own: the product of the multihoming share, the portable share, and the rival's relative value in the format must exceed a threshold. The model also shows that portable shaping can shift category-wide taste without raising the shaper's share, while specific shaping raises the shaper's share without shifting category-wide taste. A shaper facing a stronger imitator chooses more specific shaping, and a mandate that converts specific attachment into portable attachment lowers the return to shaping. A dynamic simulation shows which results survive with heterogeneous users, depreciating tastes, imitation lags, and endogenous category participation. We state five propositions, contrast them with rival mechanisms, and outline an identification agenda.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: Applied US tariffs have risen sharply since the 2018–19 US-China trade war and escalated further in 2025. Using SBCS data (2015–2025), WTO trade data, and US Census data, we examine cost-pressure heterogeneity within the small-business sector. On the extensive margin – whether a firm faces rising import costs at all (2022–2024), micro-firms (1–4 employees) report the lowest incidence (71–77%), while 10–49-employee firms report the highest (81–89%), an inverted-U pattern reflecting micro-firms' more limited import dependence. On the intensive margin – how firms respond to tariff-driven cost increases conditional on exposure (2025), micro-firms show the widest pass-through/absorption gap (19 percentage points versus 10–14 for mid-sized small businesses). A Stone-Geary cost function explains this divergence: non-substitutable input floors impose larger unavoidable cost shocks on micro-firms even when pass-through rates are similar across size classes. Manufacturing shows the highest import-cost exposure with constrained pass-through and the largest firm-count decline among benchmark sectors over 2017–2022 (−3.4%, versus −0.5% for retail). Tariffs thus create a two-stage vulnerability: most micro-firms are shielded by limited import dependence, but those exposed face markedly worse outcomes.

title: When Everyone has AI: A Theory of Marketing Advantage under Algorithmic Parity
affiliations: Eject Solutions Pvt Ltd

detail.title: When Everyone has AI: A Theory of Marketing Advantage under Algorithmic Parity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced this work.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming shared marketing infrastructure rather than a proprietary capability. If competing firms use similar platforms, models and optimization systems, why should AI remain a source of advantage? This paper introduces Algorithmic Parity, the condition in which competitors have access to functionally similar AI for targeting, bidding, content generation, optimization and measurement, and argues that under parity the marginal advantage of generic AI adoption declines while the value of scarce complements rises. It defines five complements, jointly called Differentiation Capital: brand capital, proprietary data capital, human trust capital, causal learning capital and visibility capital. It also identifies a Synthetic Content Paradox: generative AI makes content production abundant while making meaningful attention scarcer. A stylized model yields eight falsifiable propositions. An audit of published secondary evidence (platform disclosures, adoption surveys, controlled productivity experiments, consumer surveys and search studies) finds the propositions consistent in direction but directly tested in few cases. The paper therefore specifies five pre-registered studies and two new metrics to test them. No new experimental data are reported in this version. The contribution is a theory, a measurement agenda and a managerial architecture for competing when everyone has AI.

detail.abstract: Although agrifood markets were traditionally modeled as competitive, there is growing empirical evidence that these markets deviate significantly from the key axioms of perfect competition as market concentration increases among intermediaries, vertical coordination strengthens along the chain, products become increasingly differentiated, and informational asymmetries prevail between buyers and sellers. We investigate key market structure issues in modern agrifood systems in the context of developed and developing economies. We summarize canonical conceptual frameworks that are employed by economists to study the role of market structure in shaping economic outcomes in agrifood systems and discuss the theoretical and empirical insights generated by these frameworks. The literature suggests that producer and consumer welfare depend critically on market concentration, vertical market structure, product differentiation, and information availability throughout the chain. These structural features interact with and reinforce one another and should be considered jointly in the design of policies aimed at supporting farmers and consumers.

detail.abstract: As unionization has declined and social support systems have weakened, many large U.S. employers now operate Employee Hardship Funds (EHFs) --- programs providing emergency cash grants to workers, funded substantially through worker donations. Despite operating at hundreds of firms, EHFs have received no scholarly attention. Drawing on three pre-registered studies, I provide the first systematic evidence on how workers perceive EHFs and how realistic program messaging shapes their attitudes and behavioral intentions. A national survey of retail workers finds that fewer than one in four identify an EHF at their employer, even though workers value EHFs highly once described. Survey experiments at Home Depot and Walmart show that EHF messages shift union vote intentions without improving workers' perceived financial security. At Home Depot, messages about its more generous, heavily promoted program reduced interest in unionization and increased job attachment, consistent with union substitution arguments. At Walmart, messages about its more modest program reduced opposition to unions and produced no job attachment effects, the opposite of presumed employer interests. EHFs are best understood as part of a bundle of employment practices that constitute workplace governance, not as isolated interventions.

detail.abstract:
Background: Hospital systems may delegate operational work to AI agents. Whether they respect spending limits, privacy and governing on that scale and report their actions is still widely untested.

Methods: We stress-tested agents built on 14 AI models across 3,592 shifts in a simulated hospital, performing realistic operational tasks (like restoring a formulary interface). Each agent received a manager’s task, spending limits and tools. We recorded what agents tried to spend, what payments went through and what their reports included. This was tested under varied types of prompting and pressure to finalise tasks, and also under a multi-agent framework. The main outcome was whether agents took actions beyond their authority. Two blinded physicians independently reviewed a subset of 271 shifts and automated judgements. 

Findings: At baseline, agents acted beyond their authority in 93 of 2,341 shifts (3.97%, 95% CI 3.22 to 4.84). The rate rose with pressure, from none in 352 shifts without added pressure to 6.74% at the highest level. Across all experiments, agents attempted $1.48 million in unauthorised twelve-month commitments. In the tested multi-agent teams (on a subset of hard tasks from the baseline test), agents acted beyond their authority in 66.2% of shifts versus 40.6% when the same lead worked alone. In 46 of 160 team shifts, the group exceeded its total limit while each payment stayed within its per-action cap. In 38 of 91 reviewed shifts with a breach (41.8%), the agent did not accurately report it. 

Interpretation: Agents given a hospital budget exceeded their authority under ordinary pressure, and their reports did not reliably reveal it. Before delegating spending authority, health systems and regulators should require enforced payment limits, one running total per agent team and independent report checks, and test these safeguards in real hospital operations.

detail.abstract: Crisis exposure can reshape option-implied risk without a broad increase in variance. Using sector averages of individual-stock option measures for S&P 500 firms, we examine nine financial, political, pandemic, and geopolitical events between 2008 and 2023. Eventspecific exposure groups are compared at maturities of 2, 30, 60, and 91 days. We distinguish differences already present before the event from additional changes after the event. Financial and market-stress episodes combine broad variance increases with downside repricing. Political events produce opposing skewness and kurtosis adjustments, while Ukraine's clearest changes concern right-tail composition and higher moments. COVID outbreak raises downside variation. Vaccine news partly unwinds earlier variance and downside differentials, yet lower variance coexists with more negative longer-horizon skewness. Directly estimated maturity spreads reveal adjustments of opposite signs across adjacent segments, even when variance levels move in the same direction. Together, the phase and maturity comparisons reveal changes in the amount and composition of priced risk that variance or post-event estimates alone can conceal.

detail.abstract: Research on large language models (LLMs) in manufacturing has expanded rapidly, but existing studies remain dispersed across individual tasks, technologies, and operational domains. This paper reviews and synthesizes recent literature on LLM applications in manufacturing operations management (OM), organized around core decision areas including product and process design, quality management, maintenance, supply chain and inventory management, scheduling, layout design, and human resources. The review identifies two levels of contribution. At the application level, LLMs support tasks such as requirement analysis, process planning, defect diagnosis, maintenance knowledge extraction, supply chain decision support, and scheduling formulation. At the operational level, they serve as connectors between unstructured information, domain knowledge, human users, and analytical systems. Across the reviewed studies, their value lies in improving knowledge access, reducing manual effort, supporting faster decisionmaking, and enhancing responsiveness. The paper also highlights that effective use typically requires domainspecific grounding, human oversight, and transformation of end-to-end processes.

detail.abstract: The global race over Artificial Intelligence (AI) has triggered a parallel competition over regulation. Major economies are competing to shape global AI governance norms and export their values either through horizontal regulations, as the European Union does, or by 'lighttouch' intervention to foster innovation, an approach favoured by the United States and the United Kingdom. This article conducts a comparative analysis of European (European Union (EU) and United Kingdom), North American (U.S. and Canada), Russian, and Chinese policies on AI. My paper aims to answer the following question: what are the normative and philosophical foundations underlying these distinctive models of AI regulation and how is geopolitical competition affecting these models? To answer this question, I survey policy and legal documents adopted between 2016 and 2026 across six jurisdictions. My corpus includes hard law, soft law, and national strategies; supplemented by officials' public declarations. The article identifies three normative traditions: rights-based tempered by utilitarianism (EU and Canada), pragmatic-utilitarian (U.S. and UK), and collectivist (Russia and China). The central empirical finding is that there has been a rhetorical convergence towards the European model between 2019 and 2023. From 2023 until 2026, geopolitical competition has produced what I term 'instrumental convergence' towards a market-based framework, despite no normative consensus. The three models increasingly share regulatory features which obscure persisting differences in underlying values. This article makes three contributions. First, I provide an extended summary of AI policies in six countries and their evolution over time. Second, I provide a normative typology of the major AI regulatory models beyond legal instruments. Third, I document rhetorical and instrumental convergences in AI regulations, advancing hypotheses for this phenomenon. This paper aims to provide insights for policymakers and for the design of multilateral AI governance frameworks, such as those developed within the ITU, at UNESCO or the OECD. I conclude by arguing in favour of a regime of international treaties over technical harmonisation (ISO and other norms) to solve cooperation issues amid conflicting normative models. Report on AI use: Artificial intelligence tools were used at various stages of the research, such as when searching institutional literature. In some sections, I used tools such as Claude and DeepL to translate paragraphs written in French, my native language, into English.

detail.abstract: Readers of Hearts & Minds will discover that China has been patient in Latin America, that it varies its methods to suit local conditions, that it adapts, and that its efforts to shape media are coordinated with its diplomacy and investments. Some Chinese influence efforts have been ham-handed, but most have been determined and well-resourced. Spanish-language training programs are thriving in China after a long dry spell and the numbers of expatriate Chinese in the region is rising. Not all of China's attention to Latin America is nefarious. Much of it is organic and some Chinese investment lending has benefitted local populations. Even projects that do not succeed fully may win friends for China in the absence of American options. China's open or surreptitious efforts to shape Latin America opinion through media, however, are unambiguous: their aim is to build support for the Chinese Communist Party's values, policies, and power. As in Africa, this is a story not only of Chinese action but of American inaction and neglect. Hearts & Minds eschews polemics and tells these stories through well-researched case studies, interviews, and data.

detail.abstract: Human resource (HR) analytics has moved from descriptive reporting to predictive and prescriptive modelling, promising evidence-based decisions about workforce planning and performance management. This review examines peer-reviewed literature on HR analytics, covering its conceptual foundations, applications, adoption barriers, and ethical risks. The review finds that the field is rich in technical possibility but uneven in theoretical grounding and demonstrated organizational value. Three persistent problems emerge: a gap between analytical capability and strategic impact, limited attention to causal reasoning, and unresolved concerns about fairness, transparency, and employee autonomy. Building on these observations, the paper proposes a conceptual framework linking data governance, analytical methods, decision integration, and ethical oversight to workforce planning and performance outcomes. The framework is a synthesis for future empirical testing, not an empirically validated model. The paper concludes that HR analytics will deliver sustained value only when organizations treat it as a decision-making discipline, not a reporting technology, and when predictive accuracy is matched by interpretability, causal credibility, and legitimacy among the employees affected. Practical implications for HR leaders and research directions for scholars are outlined.

detail.abstract: Major rail disasters require simultaneous rescue, fatality recovery, forensic identification, family assistance and preservation of evidence. This study analyses the 28 February 2023 Tempi rail collision in Greece as an end-to-end mass-fatality management system. A documentary case-study design was used, centred on the official EODASAAM/HARSIA investigation, contemporaneous public-authority updates, INTERPOL Disaster Victim Identification guidance and WHO/ICRC protocols. Sixteen auditable requirements were assessed using a Documented Protocol Alignment Index (DPAI). Thirteen criteria were assessable (evidence coverage 81.3%). Equal-weight DPAI was 53.8%, but alignment varied sharply by stage: 16.7% for scene/recovery, 50.0% for transfer/command and 100% for selected mortuary/DVI/family functions. A criticality-weighted sensitivity analysis reduced overall alignment to 42.5%; 83.3% of the unweighted protocol deficit and 87.0% of the weighted deficit were concentrated in scene/recovery. At outcome level, human remains were attributable to 56 of 57 confirmed fatalities, giving personlevel Victim Recovery Completeness of 98.25%, but the Critical Unresolved Victim Flag remained positive (CUVF=1). Comparative analysis with Santiago de Compostela, Eschede, Amagasaki and Lac-Megantic shows that Tempi combined rapid downstream DNA identification with early closure of the principal recovery operation and weaker upstream identity anchoring. The principal safety lesson is institutional: specialist capability existed, but key functions were insufficiently integrated at the recovery-DVI-investigation-clearance interfaces.

detail.abstract: Efficient learning of inventory policies from sampled demand trajectories has been studied extensively, but understanding when and how to obtain horizon-free guarantees remains a fundamental question. We consider a $T$-period inventory problem with bounded demands and the well-studied base-stock policy class. We show that $\widetilde{O}(1/\eps)$ IID demand trajectories suffice to learn an $\eps$-optimal base-stock policy in expected average loss under temporal independence and lower-bounded demand mass, while $O(1/\eps^2)$ trajectories suffice without either assumption. Both guarantees are independent of $T$. Our analysis centers on resets in the forward inventory dynamics, through which the influence of earlier base-stock decisions vanishes, reducing the effective complexity of the policy class. For the $\widetilde{O}(1/\eps)$ bound, the two additional demand assumptions yield a quadratic growth condition and ensure that cumulative demands eliminate the influence of earlier base-stock decisions, with the probability of no reset decaying exponentially in the interval length. For the $O(1/\eps^2)$ bound previously established by Xie et al. (2026), we provide a direct proof using deterministic resets: after discretization, earlier occurrences of a given base-stock level are dominated by its most recent occurrence.

detail.abstract: This exploratory paper argues that some businesses are legally, operationally, and culturally structured in ways that better support integrative collective bargaining. It focuses on workerowned cooperatives, positing that they are more likely than traditional, non-socially responsible corporations to foster integrative bargaining. If this is correct, then the advantages of integrative collective bargaining could be more fully realized by encouraging the development of businesses such as worker-owned cooperatives. The paper draws on literature on distributive versus integrative bargaining to explain the potential benefits of integrative approaches, and on labor law and collective bargaining scholarship to identify obstacles to their use in this context. It also examines research on worker-owned cooperatives to describe their legal structure and value orientation and on interviews with individuals who have participated directly in collective bargaining in unionized worker cooperatives. Together, the literature and interviews support the view that traditional company structures discourage integrative bargaining, while cooperative structures encourage it. This paper argues that worker-owned cooperatives enable transparency and information sharing, the practice of bargaining over unlimited topics, and ongoing partnership and problem solving that result in successful integrative collective bargaining. The way a business is set up can shape how well workers and management work together during contract negotiations. Research and interviews suggest that worker-owned cooperatives make cooperative, problem-solving bargaining more likely than traditional companies, suggesting that expanding this kind of business could help workplaces reach better, fairer agreements. 2

detail.abstract: Iraq’s accession to the 1958 New York Convention via Law No. 14 of 2021 signaled a landmark transition toward integrating the state into the global dispute resolution architecture. However, treaty ratification alone has not resolved the structural tension between international enforcement obligations and the archaic arbitration framework codified in the Iraqi Civil Procedure Code No. 83 of 1969. This article examines the systemic risk of interpretive drift, whereby domestic courts nominally adhere to the Convention while importing obsolete statutory reflexes—such as excessive procedural formalism, sua sponte annulment scrutiny, and expansive public policy interpretations under Article V(2)(b). Analyzing Iraq’s three treaty reservations alongside the procedural mechanics of local courts, this study evaluates the commercialramifications for cross-border transactions, specifically along the critical Iran–Iraq trade corridor. It concludes that safeguarding the integrity of arbitral awards requires a dual reform: legislative modernization modeled after the UNCITRAL Model Law and focused judicial discipline distinguishing between enforcement proceedings and domestic merits review.

detail.abstract: Human-in-the-loop requirements assume that the presence of a reviewer produces oversight. It does not. A reviewer may lack the evidence, authority, time, or discriminative ability to tell a flawed AI recommendation from a sound one, and oversight then transfers responsibility without transferring control. This paper develops Supervisability as a systemlevel property of AI-assisted decision processes and distinguishes three quantities that existing frameworks do not consistently distinguish: the supervisory capacity a decision requires, the capacity the system makes available, and the capacity reviewers actually exercise. We model the supervisory act with signal detection theory and derive the required decision criterion from the impact and reversibility of the decision, so that risk-sensitive oversight becomes a computable target rather than a normative aspiration. Capacity is assessed through a non-compensatory rule in which any missing condition renders oversight nominal, summarized by a weakest-link Supervisability Index that identifies the binding constraint. We separate a Capacity Gap from an Exercise Gap, propose operational metrics tied to decision records, and introduce seeded-error audits to measure detection sensitivity in production despite selective labels. A worked credit example shows that a compensatory average can rate a workflow as adequate while the binding constraint, review time, drives most of the avoidable loss. Seven falsifiable propositions, including an accuracy-oversight paradox in which better models can weaken oversight, define an empirical agenda for regulated financial services and agentic systems.

detail.abstract: The rise of social media platforms, notably Instagram, has fundamentally altered the landscape of how individuals share and consume travel experiences. Instagram, with its visual-centric nature, user-generated content, and social validation mechanisms such as likes and comments, has become a powerful tool in influencing travelers' perceptions and decisions about their preferred destinations. Instagram exposes travelers to captivating imagery, personal stories, and peer recommendations, shaping their travel aspirations and preferences. Using a quantitative research methodology, this study aims to examine how Instagram hotspots influence traveler choice and how online trust functions as a mediator between Instagram hotspots and traveler choice. A sample of 384 Instagram users of Generation Y was determined as the sample size using the convenience sampling technique. Structured self-administered questionnaires were distributed to collect the primary data, and Structural Equation Modelling through Smart PLS was applied to analyze the data. The research found that Instagram hotspots significantly influence destination choice, with online trust partially mediating this relationship. This study's findings shed light on the relationship between Instagram content, user engagement, and destination choices, offering Sri Lanka's tourism stakeholders valuable insights for strategic decision-making. The insights from this study empower stakeholders to enhance their promotional strategies and resource allocation. By understanding the factors influencing travelers' choices and preferences, tourism authorities and businesses can customize their marketing campaigns, craft targeted messaging, and create engaging content that resonates with their audience. By understanding the factors that influence travelers' choices, tourism authorities and businesses can tailor their marketing campaigns, develop targeted messaging, and create engaging content that resonates with their audience.

detail.abstract: Shteynberg's (2024) work on collective consciousness offers unique and meaningful insights into consumer behavior by emphasizing a "we-representation" that is comprised not of a self-aware "I" and an external "you" but rather complete immersion as a unified "we". In this commentary, we situate collective consciousness within existing social presence research in consumer behavior and discuss its potential to expand the scope of social presence research. Specifically, we utilize a social presence framework that highlights the type of co-presence (inperson vs. virtual) and the extent of interactivity (interactive vs. passive) discussing the psychological mechanisms and linkage to collective consciousness. In addition to discussing shared consumption and shared decision-making, we assess the implications of collective consciousness for consumer contexts facilitated by virtual technologies: fake news, live streaming, virtual reality, cryptocurrencies, and crowdfunding. We conclude by highlighting future avenues for integrating collective consciousness into consumer psychology research.

detail.abstract: Purpose: This study examines how flash-sale promotional attributes influence impulse buying behaviour among Generation Z consumers in Sri Lankan online retail platforms, with Fear of Missing Out (FOMO) positioned as the internal psychological mechanism within the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-OR) framework. Design/methodology/approach: A quantitative, deductive, cross-sectional survey design was employed. An online structured questionnaire was distributed through digital channels. Of 302 responses initially collected, 57 were removed during screening, leaving 250 valid responses from adult Generation Z consumers with prior flash-sale experience. Descriptive analysis and data screening were conducted in SPSS, while reliability, validity, structural relationships, explanatory power, predictive relevance, and indirect effects were examined using PLS-SEM in SmartPLS. Findings: Urgency positively affected FOMO (β = 0.460, t = 10.204, p < 0.001), as did scarcity (β = 0.489, t = 10.931, p < 0.001). Discount depth showed a negative and non-significant relationship with FOMO (β =-0.055, t = 1.110, p = 0.267). FOMO positively affected impulse buying behaviour (β = 0.469, t = 7.930, p < 0.001). Indirect effects through FOMO were significant for urgency (β = 0.216, t = 5.639, p < 0.001) and scarcity (β = 0.229, t = 6.554, p < 0.001), but not for discount depth (β =-0.026, t = 1.079, p = 0.281). Originality/value: The study provides context-specific evidence from Sri Lanka and clarifies that time-pressure and limitedavailability cues are more closely associated with FOMO than price reduction alone in the studied Generation Z sample. It also demonstrates the importance of FOMO as a psychological pathway linking selected flash-sale stimuli with spontaneous purchasing behaviour.

detail.abstract: We study how intensely a monopolist should personalize prices when personalization erodes consumer trust. The firm chooses a scalar intensity α ∈ [0, 1] that interpolates between a uniform price (α = 0) and type-specific monopoly prices (α = 1), and must keep a trust index, which falls with perceived price unfairness, above a floor T min. With linear individual demand, profit is an exact quadratic function of α: personalization captures the fraction α(2-α) of a maximal gain ∆ equal to the aggregate demand slope B times the demand-weighted variance of ideal prices, aggregate quantity is invariant to α, and total surplus falls. Without implementation costs, trust is therefore the only force limiting personalization; with convex implementation costs the optimum is α * = min{α U , α T }, the smaller of the unconstrained profit-maximizing level and the largest trust-feasible level. We derive α T in closed form for three trust specifications, characterize the optimum through the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions, interpret the multiplier as the shadow value of trust, and derive comparative statics. When trust binds, the firm's optimal price dispersion equals a "trust budget" that does not depend on consumer heterogeneity; heterogeneity weakly raises constrained profit (strictly once the optimal intensity is positive) while lowering α * when trust binds, and α * is hump-shaped in heterogeneity once implementation costs are present. We close by listing what has been established and which extensions remain open.

detail.abstract: Shelf space is an important resource in today's retail world, especially in the fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) industry, where product visibility greatly influences consumer buying decisions. Brands often aim to match their share of shelf (SOS) with their market share to remain visible and competitive at the point of sale. This study examines the relationship between share of shelf and market share in modern retail stores through a detailed audit in Bhopal, India. It also looks into whether differences in merchandising presence impact shelf execution. Data was collected from twenty modern trade stores across various retail chains, including DMart, Reliance, Vishal Mega Mart, and Aapoorti. Shelf allocation was analyzed across five FMCG product categories for two main brands: Dabur India Ltd and Hindustan Unilever Limited (HUL), using shelf-length analysis based on photographs of retail shelves. While overall SOS values appeared broadly aligned with market share benchmarks, a closer inspection of individual chains revealed significant differences among retail formats. High throughput stores like DMart and Reliance often showed considerable under-allocation, whereas smaller chains had a tendency to over-allocate shelf space. These findings suggest that overall shelf metrics might overlook important gaps in execution. The research also shows that having more merchandising staff does not always improve shelf execution across all categories.

title: From Digital Archives to Intelligent Heritage Ecosystems: Generative AI, Digital Twins, and Immersive Technologies in Cultural Heritage Management

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific funding from any public, commercial, or not-for-profit organization.

detail.abstract: Cultural heritage institutions have spent three decades converting collections into digital form, yet most digital archives remain static repositories that people search but rarely reason over. Three technology families are now converging to change this: heritage digital twins that link physical assets to continuously updated data, generative artificial intelligence (AI) that can summarise, translate, reconstruct and narrate, and immersive technologies that place audiences and specialists inside spatial representations of heritage. This article reviews recent literature and policy developments, including systematic reviews of generative reconstruction and the European data space for cultural heritage, and proposes a five-layer, provenance-first framework for what it calls intelligent heritage ecosystems. The central argument is that value arises less from any single technology than from the semantic and governance layers that connect them. The article offers a graded verification workflow for generated content, a risk register, and a phased roadmap for institutions of differing capacity. It concludes that generative AI should be positioned as an assistive and evaluative layer under expert and community authority, rather than as an autonomous author of heritage knowledge.

title: Symbiotic Forecasting for Executive Decisions Conditional Multiple-layer 360 Cascading Forecasting

detail.title: Symbiotic Forecasting for Executive Decisions Conditional Multiple-layer 360 Cascading Forecasting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no financial or personal relationships with individuals or organizations that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Executives need forecasts that help them decide: which future conditions they may face, which
they can act on, what each decision is likely to achieve, whether their targets can be reached,
and when a forecast no longer applies. Forecasting technology has never been more powerful,
yet current systems are built from the side of the machine — data, models and planning
processes — rather than from what executives need, and the human role in them is mostly to
approve or adjust. The question is how to put this technology to work with the people who
decide, as partners, across the whole forecasting and decision process.
This paper proposes symbiotic forecasting, realised through an architecture named
Conditional Multiple-Layer 360 Cascading Forecasting. People and machines work together
from the executive’s need to revalidation: functions declare the conditions they know best;
machines project, test and monitor, show the decision maker what they ask to see and advise
what they should see before deciding; the planning body integrates; and the executive decides.
Conditions pass down decision layers from the world economy to the product and are screened
around the organisation — upstream, downstream and laterally, which is what “360” means
— with only those that bear on the target modelled, and predictive, exploratory and normative
forecasting combine within one decision, tested for feasibility on demand, supply and
competition together. The backbone that makes the partnership safe is the governance of
validity: decisions already taken travel down the chain as conditions with their validity,
historical data are read as events produced under the conditions and decisions of their time,
and learning is bounded by applicability. Because capability is of value only when it reaches
the person deciding, decision ergonomics — the fit between system and decision maker at each
step — is part of the architecture.
The author’s capability scan of fourteen contemporary systems, coded from public
documentation against twenty-six capabilities, finds what the machine contributes widely
documented, and the partnership largely partial or not established in the documentation
reviewed. A capability-based walkthrough of a chocolate-confectionery case illustrates how the
missing tests could change an executive’s decision, and the paper outlines how an integrated
system could be extended towards full symbiosis. Two instruments are proposed: a
practitioner checklist and the Symbiotic Forecasting Assessment Questionnaire.
The paper is conceptual and offered for multidisciplinary review; its scope is decisions about
products, services and their markets. It is written for researchers in forecasting, decision
science and human–machine collaboration, for whom it sets out constructs and testable
propositions; for consultants, as a diagnostic instrument; for executives and managers, as a
guide to what current applications can and cannot do for their decisions; and for software and
AI firms, as a requirements specification and an extension pathway.

title: The Invoice Coordinate Method: A Shared Language for Supplier Positions, and a Payment Tolerance Box for Paying Suppliers Under a Budget
affiliations: Independent Researcher, Geneva, Switzerland

detail.title: The Invoice Coordinate Method: A Shared Language for Supplier Positions, and a Payment Tolerance Box for Paying Suppliers Under a Budget

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: Finance teams discuss supplier accounts many times a day but lack a short, shared way to say where an account stands. This paper introduces the Invoice Coordinate Method. Its first element is a convention: the coordinate of a firm is the month of its earliest unpaid invoice and the total unpaid amount, stated in that order. Asked "What is the coordinate of Firm A?", an accountant answers "July, 7,000", and every colleague knows that 7,000 is owed and that the oldest unpaid bill dates from July. In calendar form the coordinate changes only when an invoice is booked or paid, so every change in what colleagues say can be traced to a posting. The second element is the Payment Tolerance Box, a decision method built on the coordinate map. A box defined by an age limit and a balance limit separates acceptable positions from Aging, Exposure and Critical zones; each supplier's slope gives its time to escape; a closed-form minimal payment returns it to the box; and a knapsack rule allocates the budget. In an illustrative 14-supplier case, a budget of 15,000 keeps 11 suppliers within tolerance against 8 under oldest-invoice-first, and full compliance costs 23,200 against 45,000. Across 1,000 synthetic firms, the method keeps more suppliers within tolerance than oldest-invoice-first in 98% of cases, and over twelve rolling months, in its coverage mode, it keeps more than twice the share of payables within tolerance of any conventional rule. The method is simple to say, compute and automate, and offers a transparent foundation for AI-based payables automation.

Site names were coded, and information was used for academic research purposes. Participants involved in interviews were informed about the purpose of the research and the type of information required. Artificial intelligence was used only as a support tool for data harmonization, terminology alignment, and summary preparation. The original documentary sources remained the basis of the analysis, and the use of artificial intelligence did not replace the researcher’s responsibility for interpreting the data.

detail.abstract: This study examines concessions in centralized multi-site Integrated Management Systems (IMS), focusing on the balance between adherence to centralized requirements and adaptation to local operational conditions. The research addressed two questions: which variables can be identified as measurable concessions, and under what conditions do these concessions strengthen or weaken centralization and adherence? An empirical and informative research design was used, based on 80 monthly observations from four sites. The data were harmonized across site contexts and analyzed using scatter plots, Pearson correlation, multiple linear regression, interaction analysis, and factorial plots. The findings identify Efficiency Rate, Utilization Rate, People Culture Rate, Site, and Alter Event or Uncertainty as measurable concession-related variables. The findings demonstrate that concessions should not be considered automatic losses of control or informal exceptions. They should instead be managed as measurable, justified, and continuously monitored adaptations. Centralization is most effective when it combines clear essential requirements with site-sensitive flexibility, maximizes system utilization, and strengthens employees’ understanding and ability to interact with the system.

detail.abstract: Manufacturing enterprises increasingly face pressure to synchronize production planning with shop floor execution in real time, yet traditional integration approaches often leave critical gaps between these domains. This paper examines how SAP-centric hyperautomation-the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotic process automation, process mining, and lowcode platforms-can bridge planning and execution to unlock end-to-end manufacturing agility. Drawing on a synthesis of recent literature, industry case studies, and documented SAP implementation experiences, the analysis identifies three primary integration architectures: SAP S/4HANA Production Planning and Detailed Scheduling for planning-side optimization, SAP Digital Manufacturing for execution-side visibility and control, and orchestration layers that connect these systems with legacy infrastructure and external hardware. Key findings indicate that hyperautomation initiatives in manufacturing yield measurable improvements in data quality, process consistency, and responsiveness to demand variability, though organizational factors including training adequacy and change management remain significant determinants of success. The paper concludes by identifying research gaps in certifiable automation safety and scalable hyperautomation architectures for small and medium-sized enterprises.

detail.abstract: The previous issue argued that a delegating authority pays twice for the same operational capability, and acknowledged that it had found no public study measuring it. This issue went looking for the figure. It does not exist, and the reason is more interesting than the figure itself: the British public audit institution found, through a survey covering one hundred and seven contracts, that half of the public authorities that responded keep no register of the assets of their contract. You cannot invoice what you have stopped seeing. This study reads the National Audit Office's 2020 report on PFI contract expiry and its survey of 75 English authorities (asset registers, access rights, uncooperative contractors, the perverse incentive to 'sweat' assets, expected disputes, skills), explains why the cost of rebuilding operational capability cannot be measured after the fact, and proposes a measurement protocol inspired by the counterfactual method of NIST GCR 04-867. detail.abstract: In six years, satellites have acquired maintenance, a life-extension market and a law of end of life: the last unmanageable class of assets has become manageable, and the international asset management standard, ISO 55001, becomes applicable to it at the very moment when its 2024 revision makes decision-making and data central requirements. This study maps that shift, then confronts it with its first condition: deciding the fate of an asset presupposes knowing where it is and what threatens it. Yet the operational register of the sky is kept by an American military squadron, its civilian successor very nearly failed to be born, and the powers that buy orbital assets, from the Gulf to Europe, contract for their access to someone else's information. Sovereignty over space assets is decided less by the ownership of satellites than by the keeping of the register. title: When an Answer Is No Answer: Police Commissioners, Freedom of Information, and No Systematic Traces
affiliations: University of Liverpool

detail.title: When an Answer Is No Answer: Police Commissioners, Freedom of Information, and No Systematic Traces

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is an independent researcher affiliated with the University of Liverpool and is separately employed by a large UK critical national infrastructure operator. The author conducted the research in a personal capacity; the employer had no role in its design, conduct, analysis, or reporting, and the views expressed are the author’s own.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
Asked about its own cyber oversight, a commissioner's office replied that the information “is held by the Constabulary”. The Minister of State for Policing and Crime must design a successor to these offices before they end in May 2028. Their duty is judged afterwards, not defined in advance. Judging it needs a systematic trace, a record made at the time and retrievable on request. Here lies a paradox: the bodies created to make police forces answerable mostly did not answer about their own oversight. Studies of Freedom of Information (FOI) explain divergent disclosure through records and culture. This study adds a structural account by comparing bodies that run a function with those that only oversee it.

Most forces answered at least three of five FOI questions about their own board's cyber oversight. Their commissioners, asked the same, mostly did not. This exploratory analysis covers 144 English public bodies. Over half the commissioners answered at least three of five questions with “not held” or a pointer to their force, called governance displacement. To the minister, such a reply is a dead end: nothing to judge, no way to tell whether oversight happened. The minister can ask commissioners to document every cyber decision, which risks ritual, or require only a minimum trace that can mask thin oversight. FOI disclosure has a price: some compiled replies describe how bodies escalate incidents, which a hostile actor could leverage to plan attacks on police digital systems nationwide. The minister must choose openly, not by default.

title: Public by Design? What the Anthropic-Pentagon Dispute Reveals About Organizational Purpose and Structure

detail.abstract: This essay analyzes the dispute between Anthropic and the Pentagon over military use of artificial intelligence (AI) through the lens of public administration theory. In January 2026, Anthropic was an established Pentagon contractor, and its AI product, Claude, was broadly embedded in federal and military systems. In late February, Secretary Pete Hegseth took the extraordinary step of designating Anthropic a supply chain risk after the company refused to remove restrictions on Claude's use for domestic mass surveillance and fully autonomous weapons. Against the prevailing narrative centered on corporate leadership, I argue that Anthropic's distinctive organizational design as a public benefit corporation (PBC) combined with a Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) permits credible commitments to broad public values. Although a single case cannot prove causality, I use abductive inference to synthesize concepts in administrative theory and develop a plausible explanation for this case. The 1 dispute suggests that organizational structure can plausibly create capacity for principled behavior consistent with both public interests and market success. Despite the promise of governance design, critical limitations persist, reaffirming the necessity of democratic engagement, deliberation, and accountability.

title: Speed of Intervention in Algorithmic Markets: Controlling Collusion and Stability
affiliations: University of Chicago, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and Imperial College Business School

declarations.funderStatement: NO funding

affiliations.org_name: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.abstract: Algorithmic pricing is prevalent in online marketplaces, raising concerns that learning algorithms may sustain supracompetitive outcomes. We study two sellers in a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma who delegate decisions to memoryless value-based learning algorithms. A platform steers demand toward sellers choosing the more competitive action. Using a fluid approximation, we characterize how intervention intensity, learning architecture, and implementation speed determine market dynamics. Stronger intervention lowers cooperation levels at the fixed point. Algorithmic responsiveness determines the location of stationary outcomes, while action-dependent learning rates determine their local stability. As intervention intensifies, the fixed point can lose stability through a Hopf bifurcation and its local basin of attraction shrinks as the stability threshold is approached. Consequently, an abrupt intervention may leave inherited Q-values outside the target's local basin of attraction and lead to persistent oscillations, whereas gradual intervention leads to a stable market outcome. We also derive local bounds on implementation speed and rollout time. Our results show that platform regulation of algorithmic collusion may require choosing not only how much to intervene, but also how quickly to implement the intervention relative to the algorithms' learning dynamics.

detail.abstract: While conventional models of household finance often presume a direct causal sequence from financial literacy to capital accumulation, empirical realities in emerging economies reveal a persistent gap between cognitive knowledge and everyday practice. This paper investigates the behavioural patterns, psychosocial drivers, and structural constraints that dictate long-term household wealth retention. Grounded in the Integrated-Flexible Approach (IFA) and operationalised through the 10Ps Research Framework, this study synthesises practical insights on unostentatious financial routines ("quiet habits") with empirical literature on investor psychology, behavioural finance, and macroeconomic structure. The inquiry explores how controlled spending, precautionary emergency funds, productive debt utilization, tax discipline, and long-term asset allocation interact with social pressure and extreme wealth inequality. The findings demonstrate that household financial resilience is rarely the product of isolated, high-yield speculative moves; rather, it is sustained by iterative, habituated routines that operate as psychological buffers against macroeconomic volatility. Furthermore, the analysis highlights that individual agency must be evaluated alongside systemic inequality, where lower-income tiers face severe structural boundaries that constrain traditional saving directives.

title: Shorter mRNA Lead Times and the Option to Wait in Influenza Vaccine Design
affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University

detail.title: Shorter mRNA Lead Times and the Option to Wait in Influenza Vaccine Design

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: Seasonal influenza vaccine composition must be chosen months before the viruses that dominate the coming season are fully known. FDA approval of the first U.S. mRNA seasonal influenza vaccine makes shorter production lead times relevant: mRNA production may take two to three months versus roughly six months for conventional production. We develop a dynamic optimalstopping model, calibrated with U.S. A(H3N2) data, to study how shorter lead time affects composition timing and flexibility. Shorter lead time creates a state-contingent option to wait rather than simply moving the decision to a later calendar date; we separate its premium over fixed timing into pure adaptivity and a fixed-date selection penalty. Waiting can be optimal even when expected antigenic match between a vaccine strain and a circulating strain deteriorates, and the value of flexibility can peak at an intermediate rather than the worst initial mismatch. The main timing conclusions extend to capped and uncapped random-yield models. Holding the target quantity fixed, reducing the production lead time from 26 to 13 weeks increases expected match-adjusted vaccine availability by 5.38%. Although immediate freezing is the best common fixed date, tailoring a fixed freezing date each season based on the initial state explains most of the adaptive policy's gain. Retrospective evidence shows that a fixed three-month delay is not consistently better, underscoring that faster mRNA production provides the option-not the obligation-to wait.

detail.abstract: We study how investments in emerging technologies reshape firm hierarchies. Extending Garicano's (2000) knowledge-based model, we distinguish between emerging information technologies (EIT) and robots (RT), and derive testable hypotheses on their effects on hierarchical depth and span of control, driven by changes in information costs, learning costs, and production predictability. Using longitudinal firm-level data from Italy (2014-2021), we find that EIT investments increase depth and reduce span of control relative to non-investing firms, while RT increase span of control when combined with EIT. Our layer-level analysis shows that EIT are associated with the addition of managerial and middle-management layers, whereas RT are associated with the addition of middlemanagement layers and the removal of top management layers; moreover, EIT reduce span of control at higher levels, while RT expand it among blue-and white-collar workers. Results are robust to alternative estimators, anticipatory-effect tests, investment switchers, common support restrictions, and alternative clustering.

detail.abstract: The world’s biggest shared problems are funded through a cycle of constant asking: securing commitments, chasing contributions, and starting over for money that may not come again. It’s a costly model that is expensive to maintain, increasingly difficult to sustain, and vulnerable to political change. This paper proposes the World Philanthropy Funding Framework (WPFF), a mandated levy equal to 1% of the processing fees that payment companies already earn from digital retail transactions. The levy is assessed once per transaction, on the fee the merchant already pays. It is collected through existing payment settlement processes and routed to a pooled philanthropy fund. Consumers see no new charge, no prompt, and no change at checkout. WPFF is designed to address four structural weaknesses in how philanthropy is funded: the friction of active solicitation, the limited scale of voluntary giving, desensitisation compounding donor fatigue, and instability, where funding remains vulnerable to national budget cycles. This paper sets out a payment architecture the levy attaches to, a phased implementation strategy, and a proposed governance and funding model to establish a structural, self-sustaining funding mechanism to transform global philanthropy from a fragile voluntary effort into a permanent global public good.

title: Policy Reforms to Unlock the Potential of Small Cells for the AI/6G Future

detail.abstract:
This paper explains how a new radio design with appropriate regulatory reforms can help drive the necessary transition to lower power, small cell wireless architectures. 

Wireless is the central nervous system for our AI economy. A significant shift in the deployed technology and the corresponding regulatory environment - our "6G future" - is necessary to realize AI's potential for enhancing economic growth and sustaining US global competitiveness. 

The need for smaller-cell architectures to support ubiquitous coverage at distances at middle ranges of a few tens of meters up to a few kilometers is especially important and has the potential to substantially alter the economics for deploying and operating edge-networks and the services those support. Although the need to transition to smaller-cell architectures for edge network providers has been clear for a long time, the densification of edge network radio access network (RAN) infrastructure in the US has been hampered by two factors-one economic and one technological. 

The economic factor stems from how the siting of cellular antennas is regulated in the US. In some regions outside the US with different regulatory processes the densification of the cellular network down to 80-m and 100-m cell sizes is already common. The second factor that has been constraining densification is technological. Fundamentally, legacy radio designs use too much power to reliably transmit digital bits. Because of this, each cell broadcasts significant "co-channel interference" into all the neighboring cells using the same frequency. Developments in three areas critical to the design of radios for edge-network communications have made it feasible to build and commercially deploy radios that significantly alleviate this problem (see https://eridan.io/). Exploiting these advances enables radios capable of matching state of the art data throughput performance with hundred-fold reduced co-channel interference and much greater energy efficiency. While an important technical barrier to wider deployment of small cells has been significantly reduced, additional regulatory and policy steps to reduce structural impediments to densification and smaller cell networks are important for enabling the transition to lower-power, smaller-cell wireless networks.

title: Corporate Procurement of Renewable Electricity: Annual versus Hourly Matching
affiliations: Imperial College Business School, Aalto University School of Business and Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business

detail.title: Corporate Procurement of Renewable Electricity: Annual versus Hourly Matching

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
