detail.abstract: In 1949, jurimetrics was forged as a coin, and for three-quarters of a century its tradition held a single face upward: measurement and prediction. This article turns that same coin to its other face, and introduces the field that stands there-AI-Based Jurimetrics. Resting upon, and without repeating, the founding declaration of this field, the article contributes three things. First, it places the field within the jurimetrics tradition: from the coining of the term by Loevinger (1949) and the founding of the journal by Layman Allen in 1959 as Modern Uses of Logic in Law under the American Bar Association-now Jurimetrics: The Journal of Law, Science, and Technology, the official journal of the ABA Section of Science & Technology Law-through the mid-century pioneers who sought to predict judicial decisions mathematically (Kort, Lawlor, Nagel, Schubert) and the early critique they drew (Fisher), down to contemporary computational legal studies (Katz, Bommarito, Blackman; Ruhl). Second, it shows that this entire lineage worked a single face of jurimetrics-measurement and prediction-whereas this field turns the coin's other face: not predicting what a court will decide, but upholding the integrity of legal research itself in the age of artificial intelligence, through non-negotiable primary-source verification, a single substantive authority vested in the human, an open inventory of technique, and disciplined continuity across sessions. Third, it anchors the field's compass in a distinctively Indonesian legal thought-Satjipto Rahardjo's progressive law (hukum progresif)-whose ideal of substantive justice, on this article's reading, halts at the level of aspiration; the field offers a disciplined, testable method so that the ideal may grow from embryo toward practice. The article positions the field against the contemporary predictive landscape, asks whether it is a science or merely a method-treating that as an open hypothesis-and deliberately builds a foothold for those who would challenge it. What it offers is not a crown but a pledge: dated, and open to testing.

detail.abstract: The literature on the impact of Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) on monetary policy transmission remains inconclusive. This paper studies how CBDC affects monetary policy transmission across advanced economies (AEs) and emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs), with a two-agent New Keynesian (TANK) model featuring active Ricardian and passive Ricardian households. Active Ricardian households hold a diversified portfolio of deposits, bonds, and risky assets, while passive Ricardians hold only deposits and participate only in the banking sector. Deposit rates are set by banks with market power, and CBDC is introduced through a money-in-utility framework with a shopping-time channel and transaction costs on deposits. We combine two features not studied together before: the distinction between active and passive Ricardian households, based on their access to bond markets, and bank market power over deposit and lending rates. For active Ricardians, monetary policy works through the spread between deposit and bond returns, and greater bank market power pushes them toward bonds. For passive Ricardians, higher policy rates raise substitution from deposits into CBDC unless banks reduce market power and pass more through to deposit rates. Because active Ricardian households make up about two thirds of households in our AE calibration but only around a sixth in our EMDE calibration, CBDC weakens the deposit, bank lending, asset price and wealth channels of monetary policy in AEs while strengthening them in EMDEs; the new monetarist channel strengthens in both. As the transaction cost on use of deposits for payment transaction rises, both types of household shift more of their liquid balances into CBDC. Even a moderate, positive transaction charge on deposits, which is levied on the households, is enough to raise CBDC uptake in that economy. We also find that the introduction of CBDC in EMEs increases the volatility of output, investment and inflation, while it reduces volatility in the AEs.

detail.abstract: This paper documents that overreaction to news in inflation expectations is a common feature of individual-level forecasting across five categories of economic agents: households, firms, professional forecasters, policymakers, and experimental participants. We show that the overreaction parameter is consistently negative, with mean individual coefficients of similar magnitude across different institutional contexts, data sources and forecast frequencies. We also document that inflation experience correlates with overreaction for all categories, dampening it for professional forecasters and firms, consistent with learning, but amplifying it for policymakers, households and experimental participants, consistent with credibility concerns, salience or memory effects.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the structural application of tokenisation and distributed ledger technology (DLT) to asset administration pipelines within alternative investment funds (AIFs), moving beyond conventional retail distribution use cases. While current industry applications focus on front-end tokenised feeder vehicles, this paper explores high-value, multi-leg operational processes: contributions in kind, inter-domicile fund migrations, and secondary transfers of private fund interests. Utilizing recent institutional frameworks from the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) and the Financial Stability Board (FSB), the paper models the transition from fragmented, linear intermediary workflows to a state-conditional, interoperable DLT architecture. By mapping case reconstructions from German and Luxembourgish fund structures, the paper demonstrates that the core operational logic of alternative asset administration can be programmatically embedded within smart contracts to achieve atomic settlement. The paper concludes with a strategic pilot framework for financial market infrastructure providers, advocating for a sequenced adoption model that prioritizes asset-ready transactions, such as listed securities contributions settled via wholesale central bank digital currency links, without disrupting the legally mandated oversight functions of alternative investment fund managers, depositaries, and transfer agents.

detail.abstract: In liberal democracies, the inability of voters to enforce campaign pledges represents an agency problem, as politicians can make non-binding promises during elections without incurring ex ante costs. This paper introduces an economic model of mandatory liability insurance for political campaign promises. Under this framework, candidates running for office must obtain liability insurance for at least one quantifiable policy target. Insurance companies screen candidates and assess risks, setting individualized premiums paid by the candidates that reflect candidate credibility, expertise, and policy feasibility. Insurance details are disclosed to the electorate, providing voters with additional information. After the election, an independent evaluation body determines whether the promised thresholds have been met. If a promise is not fulfilled, the insurer pays financial compensation into a public fund. Political liability insurance thus offers a potential solution to the problem of unenforceable campaign promises, promoting a more transparent and accountable electoral process.

detail.abstract: Using proprietary granular data on human–AI interactions, we study how investors acquire information through AI tools and how AI-assisted information acquisition affects investor disagreement. We first document a striking topic persistence in investors’ information acquisition: for the same stock, investors are ten times more likely to continue searching for information on the same topic as their initial query, and this persistence is accompanied by little informational gain. These findings suggest a behavioral bias in investors’ information acquisition. We also find that investors’ disagreement increases as conversations progress. Decomposing overall disagreement, we show that within-topic disagreement decreases, while between-topic disagreement increases, and it is the latter that drives the rise in overall disagreement.

detail.abstract: This paper quantifies the impacts of public research funding on research output and characterizes its optimal allocation across research fields. We estimate the effect of U.S. federal research funding on research output in 196 STEM fields over 1999-2020, exploiting variation generated by interactions between field-specific exposure to defense spending and aggregate defense spending shocks. Our estimates indicate an elasticity of research output with respect to funding of 0.349. We then develop a parsimonious dynamic model of knowledge accumulation and diffusion to characterize the optimal allocation of public research funding. We discipline the model by the estimated elasticity, the knowledge network revealed by cross-field paper citations, and the funding priorities measured using OSTP-OMB R&D Priority Memoranda. Counterfactual analysis suggests that reallocating existing federal research funding according to the optimum raises steady-state research output by 8.2%, translating into a 12% increase in steady-state real GDP, without increasing aggregate spending. The gains arise because optimal funding disproportionately targets fields that are central to the knowledge network, whereas observed allocations underweight knowledge diffusion.

detail.abstract: Expansionary corporate events can strengthen local housing demand, but they may also induce credit reallocation from households to firms. We study the impact of this tension on housing markets using leveraged buyouts (LBOs), which generate immediate corporate financing needs but affect home purchasing power only gradually. Using U.S. county-level data and a stacked difference-indifferences design, we find that LBO activity lowers the annual house price growth rate by 3-14% over the following three years. Local bank lending shifts toward businesses and mortgage denial rates rise, corroborating the credit-reallocation mechanism. The effects are stronger for larger buyouts, in more concentrated banking markets, and in counties with more volatile house prices. The results show that housing market responses to corporate activity depend on the balance between demand spillovers and credit-reallocation forces.

detail.abstract: Implied stock-market volatility is widely used to identify uncertaintyshocks and discipline models of their macroeconomic effects. This paper gives distributional content to the option-price variation underlying these exercises. A normalized at-the-money forward put price, the Downside Protection Premium (DPP), closely tracks the VIX and preserves the principalmacroeconomic responses in the specifications examined. Its price and local strike slope separate risk-neutral shortfall probability from conditional severity. Severity accounts for almost all monthly premium comovement and 91.5 percent of the recession log premium.Conditional gains also rise substantially, while conditional losses remain larger in phase averages. Despite this severity dominance, quotations across strikes frequently exclude a common-scale explanation, conditional on the maintained forward and premium construction. Realized-volatility and future-volatility-news innovations both raise protection costs primarily through severity, yet produce different estimated employment responses in common impact-severity units; simultaneous significance depends on the inference formulation. Together, these findings supply joint empirical restrictions on theconnection between uncertainty, option prices, and economic activity.

detail.abstract: This study examined the impact of climate change on agricultural output in Nigeria over the period 1986-2024. The study specifically investigated the effects of carbon dioxide emissions, rainfall, temperature, land use and population growth on agricultural output and examined whether the interaction between climate change and land use influences agricultural output. Annual time-series data were obtained from the World Development Indicators and Food and Agriculture Organization statistical databases. An ex-post facto research design was adopted, while the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) bounds-testing framework was employed to estimate short-run and long-run relationships. The Augmented Dickey-Fuller test indicated a mixture of I(0) and I(1) variables, with none integrated at I(2), supporting the use of ARDL. The bounds test produced an F-statistic of 3.860008, exceeding the 5% upper critical bound of 3.28 and indicating a long-run relationship among the variables. The estimated errorcorrection coefficient was-0.403270 and statistically significant, implying an adjustment speed of approximately 40.3% per year toward long-run equilibrium. In the short run, carbon dioxide emissions had a statistically significant negative effect on agricultural output, while temperature also had a significant negative contemporaneous effect. The climate-change-land-use interaction was positive and significant contemporaneously but negative and significant at subsequent lags. In the long run, carbon dioxide emissions, rainfall, temperature and population growth had negative but statistically insignificant coefficients, whereas land use had a positive and statistically significant coefficient. Granger-causality results indicated no causal relationship between carbon dioxide emissions and agricultural output, while agricultural output unidirectionally Granger-caused temperature and a bidirectional relationship existed between land use and agricultural output. The findings highlight the importance of climate-smart agriculture, irrigation, resilient production systems and improved land-use management in strengthening Nigeria's agricultural resilience.

title: Diagnostic Dynamics of Redistribution Capability in Adaptive Liquidity Systems

detail.abstract: This paper studies the finite-time diagnosis of Redistribution Capability in deterministic adaptive liquidity systems when the capability being diagnosed may itself evolve during the diagnostic process. Let z t ∈ Z denote a dynamically sufficient underlying state, let C t = Γ(z t) denote the Redistribution Capability induced by that state, and let o t = O(z t) denote the observation available to an observer. Previous work distinguished current capability information from information sufficient for capability evolution and established exact deterministic identifiability criteria for redistribution-relevant state completion. The present paper addresses a different problem: how justified hypotheses about Redistribution Capability evolve as information accumulates while Redistribution Capability itself may simultaneously transform. For a target time τ and an information time t ≥ τ , the paper introduces the Diagnostic Capability Set D τ |t , consisting of all capability structures at time τ compatible with the information available through time t. A context-relative counterpart is defined over equivalence classes induced by immediate redistribution-relevant possibilities. This twotime construction separates the time of the capability being diagnosed from the time at which diagnostic information becomes available. Three principal results follow. First, capability dynamics and diagnostic dynamics are distinct: diagnostic information about a fixed capability may refine without transformation of that capability, while capability may transform without the transformation being immediately resolved diagnostically. Second, capability-change event sets and associated detection times are introduced, and a constructive result shows that finite capabilitychange detection lag can be arbitrarily long. Third, diagnostic protocols are related to capability recoverability. If distinct initial capability hypotheses remain indistinguishable under every finite protocol that keeps both branches within their respective capabilityrecoverability regions, then every exact finite diagnostic protocol must cross a recoverability boundary on at least one compatible branch. A finite deterministic construction establishes a stronger case. There exists a system in which the diagnostic intervention is the only source of exact separation and every exact finite diagnostic protocol necessarily causes an irreversible immediate capability contraction on every initially compatible branch. Exact retrospective knowledge of the initial capability is therefore obtained only after the capability being diagnosed has become unrecoverable. The results distinguish capability transformation, diagnostic information, detection, diagnosis, and recoverability as separate structural properties of adaptive liquidity systems.

detail.abstract: Evaluating the structural stability of the relationships between inflation, unemployment, and interest rates is vital for central banks striving to fulfill their dual mandates within an evolving economic landscape. This study evaluates whether the empirical dynamics governing these fundamental macroeconomic relationships have undergone significant parameter shifts over the past quarter century. Utilizing quarterly US macroeconomic data from 2001 to 2025, this study employs a recursive vector autoregression (VAR) framework that incorporates the federal funds rate alongside broader measures of labor market slack: the U6 unemployment rate) and decomposed price pressures (demand-driven inflation). Information criteria definitively show that this model offers a superior empirical fit, while the resulting impulse response functions reveal a weak, unstable response of unemployment to policy shocks that directly contradicts traditional historical benchmarks. Ultimately, this study contributes to the literature by demonstrating that fixed-parameter linear frameworks lack the structural robustness required to capture modern post-pandemic macroeconomic interactions, highlighting a critical need for time-varying analytical models.

detail.abstract: IFRS S2 and the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) require companies to disclose climate-related opportunities as well as risks. Whether the two sides are disclosed with comparable breadth and depth is not known. This working paper reports a pilot study of 36 reports under first-cycle ISSB-aligned mandates (Australia, Hong Kong, Malaysia, Sri Lanka), the ESRS and voluntary regimes. An AI coder identified 281 risk and opportunity items and scored each on identification, quantification, monetization and likelihood. Opportunities make up a median 30% of a report's items, and 26 of 32 reports with an inventory list more risks than opportunities. Overall depth is similar on both sides, but the framing differs: 40% of opportunity items carry no likelihood language, against 10% of risk items, and opportunity figures mostly report money committed or revenue earned rather than an estimated effect. Mandatory reports always contain an inventory and tend to show deeper risk disclosure, but not deeper opportunity disclosure, and depth does not rise with firm size. Risks are itemized and opportunities are asserted. All results are exploratory: they rest on a single AI coding pass that a pre-specified human-validation study will now test, and they may change.

detail.abstract:
Video games have evolved beyond a pastime for children. For decades, video game developers were mainly concerned with functionality. As technology has advanced, developers are able to focus more on the artistic qualities of their creations. Today, many gamers buy and play video games for the quality of the aesthetics and underlying messages. But these advancements have also allowed the technologically adept to alter video games. Some alterations—mods—are motivated by fans looking to exercise their own creative expression; other alterations—cheats—are implemented to make gameplay easier. Depending on the nature of the alteration, it changes the way a developer’s creative expression is conveyed and received. In extreme cases, alteration harms a developer’s honor or reputation.

The Visual Artists Rights Act (VARA) protects the moral rights of copyright authors, but only those that delve into the “fine arts.” Authors of audiovisual works, such as video game developers, are pointedly excluded from moral protection. This Note argues for the expansion of VARA to include such authors and proposes language to adequately limit modding and prohibit the use of cheats.

detail.abstract: Global climate change is the defining structural crisis of our time, forcing us to rethink how we coordinate policies, science, finance, and industrial engineering. This paper looks closely at how engineering and economic structures drive both sides of the climate equation: cutting emissions (mitigation) and building endurance (adaptation). While traditional engineering old guards spent over a century powering a fossil-fuel economy, modern technological innovations offer the primary mechanisms for decarbonization. By analyzing everything from utility-scale clean energy grids to early-stage carbon capture systems, this study maps out what works, what is lagging, and who is driving innovation-from sovereign states and corporations to the pioneering scientists themselves. Most importantly, we examine the steep economic barriers and capital asymmetries that keep these vital tools out of reach for developing regions, particularly Africa. We find that while our technical solutions are highly capable, they will fail to meet global climate targets without a radical overhaul of international project finance, localized technology transfers, and cross-border economic alignments.

detail.abstract: An influential argument against sweatshop wages holds that employers have a duty to assist disadvantaged workers and that the wages they offer fulfil this duty only partially (Berkey, 2021). In this article, we suggest that the argument holds when the benefit owed is indivisible, but that, when it can be shared, the duty may instead require employing more disadvantaged people rather than paying higher wages to those already employed. detail.abstract: This article examines the constitutional implications of Quebec’s Act respecting the laicity of the State (Bill 21), focusing on the preemptive invocation of section 33 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, commonly known as the notwithstanding clause. It argues that Bill 21 raises fundamental questions about the durability of constitutional rights, the limits of legislative supremacy and the protection of religious minorities within Canada's constitutional framework. Although framed as a neutral measure regulating religious symbols in public employment, the legislation disproportionately affects individuals whose religious practices require visible expressions of faith, particularly Muslim women, Sikh men and observant Jews. Drawing comparisons with American constitutional protections for religious freedom and equality, the article examines the tension between state neutrality, substantive equality and religious pluralism. It further considers the implications of increasingly routine and preemptive legislative overrides for judicial review, democratic accountability and constitutional culture. Ultimately, the article argues that Bill 21 represents more than a dispute over secularism or religious expression: it tests whether constitutional rights remain meaningful constraints on governmental power or become protections subject to political discretion.

EGARCH-t achieves the "best" descriptive BIC for all three indices, and most importantly, in all 24 matched comparisons, the EGARCH family also achieves lower values of the pinball loss than the GJR alternatives. In the nine comparisons where Diebold-Mariano tests reject equal predictive accuracy, they never favour GJR. The ranking is not purchased through undercoverage since all five econometric specifications pass the unconditionalcoverage and independence tests and EGARCH-EVT achieves one per cent VaR which is 2.44 to 6.43 basis points less conservative in calm states and 8.88 to 14.33 basis points less conservative in turbulent states with identical numbers of violations in each cell of the index and state matrix. Nevertheless, a histogram gradient-boosting quantile learner is fitted with fixed settings and lagged market features and refitted on the same real-time schedule and fails unconditional coverage on both of the tail levels for each index showing a calibration failure for this specification. If the contest was restricted to GARCH and GJR then the wrong family was crowned in every cell. Because the empirical results are limited to one exchange, with three indices that have overlapping constituents and share the same institutional environment, the design principle that they derive is general.

detail.abstract: Organisations have begun to purchase reasoning the way they long purchased electricity: metered, priced per token and elastic on demand. Large language models sold through per-token interfaces let a firm dial the depth of machine deliberation applied to any problem, from a shallow single pass to prolonged multi-step reasoning, at a price that scales with depth. Management theory is unprepared for this. Its foundational treatments assume cognition is scarce because human attention is scarce, and its resource theories treat computational capacity as background infrastructure rather than as a governed input to advantage. This conceptual paper introduces the construct of governed cognitive capacity, defined as an organisation's metered stock of machine deliberation together with the routines that shape its demand, allocate its depth and assure its outputs. Drawing from resource orchestration, the attention-based view, bounded rationality and the emerging literatures on delegation to agentic artefacts, six propositions are developed linking capacity governance to value capture, including an inverted-U relation between deliberation depth and net value conditional on output verifiability, an allocation-not-access locus of competitive advantage and a transaction-cost boundary for external agent services. A three-plane governance framework - demand shaping, allocation and assurance - organises the propositions for practice. Contributions to theory, implications for managers and an operationalisation agenda are discussed.

detail.abstract:
It is well known that monetary policy affects firms' investment decisions. But which firms are the most responsive to changes in interest rates? And does this responsiveness vary over time? The literature has given diverse answers to this question, focusing on characteristics such as firm size, age, and financial position, and mostly studying these traits in isolation. In this post based on a recent Staff Report, we explore how investment responsiveness to monetary policy changes across firms and over time. We find that investment by most firms in most time periods responds little to monetary policy. For some firms in some periods, however, investment is very responsive to changes in interest rates. While these instances of strong sensitivity correlate with several firm traits, there is substantial variation that cannot easily be linked to specific characteristics of firms. Our findings therefore underscore the importance of considering the entire distribution of investment responses rather than focusing on the average effect. How Firms' Investment Responds to Changes in Monetary Policy Our analysis revisits a burgeoning literature that estimates how firm-level investment responds to monetary policy surprises. In particular, we build on influential work by Ottonello and Winberry (2020). Monetary policy surprises are measured as changes in the federal funds rate implied by federal funds futures in a narrow window around monetary policy announcements. Investment is the growth rate in the capital stock measured at a quarterly frequency for each publicly listed firm in Compustat. The literature has typically studied heterogeneity in investment responses by interacting monetary surprises in a regression framework with a chosen firm characteristic, such as size, age, or a particular financial variable.

To view post: https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org/2026/10/firm-heterogeneity-and-the-response-of-investment-to-monetary-policy/

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is no longer approaching. It has arrived. Yet organizations continue to treat AI's institutionalization as a future problem, even as individuals, teams, and entire generations already live and work inside AI-enhanced environments. This chapter examines the paradox at the heart of modern management: the same employees who use AI fluently in their personal lives are met with institutional contradiction, and sometimes opposition, when they bring AI-enhanced ideas and tools to work. Drawing on resource-based theory, absorptive capacity, and emerging empirical data, this chapter argues that the AI-inclusive manager is not a replacement for human judgment but its amplifier. It posits that organizations which systematize AI as an integral resource configuration, rather than treating it as an add-on or a threat, can build durable competitive advantage. Those that do not will not merely fall behind. They will find themselves increasingly outpaced, the gap widening, and closing it harder each year. The chapter concludes with an examination of what remains irreplaceable: the human attention, human filters of experience, relational intelligence, and ethical discernment through which AI's encyclopedic output becomes wisdom. Without human expertise and discernment, AI is not wisdom; it is volume.

detail.abstract: The manufacturing landscape is undergoing a profound transformation driven by the convergence of enterprise resource planning systems, advanced planning platforms, and intelligent automation technologies. This paper examines the convergence of SAP Production Planning, SAP Integrated Business Planning, and intelligent automation technologies in shaping the future of manufacturing operations. As manufacturers confront increasingly complex challenges including demand volatility, supply chain disruptions, shortening product lifecycles, and rising customer expectations for customization and delivery speed, the integration of these three technological domains offers a pathway toward more responsive, efficient, and resilient manufacturing systems. This research investigates the synergistic relationships between SAP Production Planning, which provides the transactional infrastructure for material requirements planning, capacity management, and production execution; SAP Integrated Business Planning, which offers advanced analytics, demand sensing, and integrated supply chain planning capabilities; and intelligent automation technologies, including machine learning, robotic process automation, and artificial intelligence, which enable autonomous decision-making and adaptive process optimization. The study employs a conceptual analysis approach, synthesizing insights from the academic literature, industry reports, and practitioner accounts to develop a comprehensive framework for understanding how these technologies converge to create new manufacturing capabilities. The framework identifies three convergence dimensions: data convergence, which addresses the integration of transactional and analytical data across planning horizons; process convergence, which examines the alignment of strategic, tactical, and operational planning processes; and intelligence convergence, which explores the application of machine learning and artificial intelligence across the planning stack. The research findings suggest that organizations that successfully integrate these technologies can achieve significant improvements in forecast accuracy, inventory optimization, production responsiveness, and overall operational efficiency. However, the research also identifies substantial challenges, including data quality requirements, integration complexity, skills gaps, and organizational change management demands, that must be addressed to realize the full potential of convergence. The paper concludes by proposing a maturity model for assessing organizational readiness for convergence and outlining a roadmap for incremental adoption. The implications for practitioners and researchers are discussed, and directions for future investigation are identified.

detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become embedded in the day-today work of knowledge professionals, offering substantial gains in productivity and efficiency. However, the self-evaluative emotional processes that knowledge workers experience when using AI remain underexplored. This research examines how AI use influences perceived ownership of task output and how such changes are associated with negative self-conscious emotions, including guilt, shame, and embarrassment. Across one pilot quasi-experiment, one pre-registered correlational study, and three pre-registered experiments (N = 2,313) using diverse samples and task contexts, individuals who had access to an AI tool during task completion-whether performing a standardized online task or an occupation-matched task-reported lower task ownership (Study 1), which was associated with heightened negative self-conscious emotions (Studies 2-3). Two further preregistered experiments embedding a live AI tool in a real, incentivized work task (Studies 4a-4b) established these effects causally and showed that legitimizing AI use through endorsement did not buffer-if anything, it deepened-the loss of ownership. This research advances our understanding of AI in organizations by highlighting how such tool can unintentionally diminish psychological ownership and shape self-evaluative emotional experience.

detail.abstract: This paper includes an introduction and a transcript of a three-part video course focused on the Pragmatic Theory of the Firm. This way of thinking evolved from my research on the life-cycle framework for connecting firms' performance to market valuations and shareholder returns plus detailed analyses of firms' (historical) life-cycle track records. detail.abstract: This paper examines how Chinese equity markets react to government procurement contracts. We find that procurement announcements are associated with significantly negative abnormal returns: the Fama-French three-factor CAR is-0.258% over [-2, +2] trading days and-0.729% over [-5, +5]. The negative response is concentrated among high-Tobin's-Q firms, while low-Q firms earn positive abnormal returns. Non-state-owned firms react more negatively than state-owned firms. Negative returns appear both before and after announcements and around non-overlapping signing windows, consistent with gradual repricing rather than a single day-0 shock. High-Q firms' cash holdings fall and long-term debt rises after announcements, consistent with contract execution absorbing cash and requiring financing. Overall, these findings suggest that an apparently favorable government contract may be bad news for suppliers whose valuations embed high growth expectations.

detail.abstract: When a household member migrates, which of the people left behind change their paid work? This paper answers with the monthly Listening to the Citizens of Uzbekistan panel, comparing the same person across months with and without a member abroad, with person and round fixed effects. Migrants are mostly sons: 62% of the 1,402 members flagged abroad are children of the household head and 20% are heads. Resident women and sons do not change their recorded paid work; the estimates rule out falls larger than 1 and 1.5 percentage points. Household heads, the migrants' fathers, are 2 to 4 percentage points less likely to work for pay while a member is abroad (two-way estimate 3.3, SE 1.4, base 51%), and 4.6 percentage points in months when a remittance arrives. The gap closes once the migrant returns. Household earned income falls 16 percentage points on the extensive margin. Food insecurity does not change.

detail.abstract: This study examines how perceived organizational culture, institutional sector, and employee compensation relate to job satisfaction and organizational commitment in Indian higher education institutions (HEIs). Conducting a secondary analysis on an open-access dataset of teaching and administrative personnel in hospitality and tourism academia (N = 386), the study evaluates bivariate associations, sectoral differences, and income-based variations across employee attitudes. Perceived organizational culture (measured via the 8-dimension OCTAPACE framework) demonstrated a moderate positive relationship with job satisfaction (r = .43, p < .001) and a modest positive association with organizational commitment (r = .23, p = .001). Sector comparisons revealed that government university employees reported significantly higher organizational commitment than private university employees (z = 3.05, p = .002), despite no statistically significant difference in perceived culture scores between sectors (p = .827). Furthermore, one-way ANOVAs confirmed that compensation tiers significantly differentiate both job satisfaction (p < .001) and commitment (p = .031). These findings suggest that while immediate job attitudes are closely tied to workplace culture, deeper organizational attachment in HEIs is strongly shaped by structural and compensation mechanisms. Practical implications for higher education governance and human resource strategies are discussed.

detail.abstract: Online resource allocation is a central problem in Operations Research, Economics, and Computer Science, where m limited shared resources must be allocated among n sequentially arriving requests with stochastic, non-identical distributions. Classical near-optimal policies assume full knowledge of these distributions. Can near-optimal posted prices instead be learned from limited feedback, and how does the answer change as prices are restricted from dynamic to anonymous to static? We study two forms of information access: historical samples and pricing queries (which reveal only what a fresh request purchases at posted prices). Our results hold for sufficiently large budgets. First, dynamic prices are learnable from a single sample. We introduce a novel Exponential Pricing algorithm that achieves a (1-ϵ)-approximation from just one sample from each of the n request distributions. This is the first finite-sample (1-ϵ)-approximation for non-identical distributions. Exponential Pricing also yields near-optimal guarantees for outliers, given a coarse estimate of the uncorrupted optimum, and for value augmentations, given the base distributions. Second, given a coarse estimate of the optimal value, polynomially many pricing queries suffice to learn a near-optimal anonymous pricing rule without solving the configuration linear program or assuming genericity. Third, polynomially many samples suffice to learn a near-optimal static price for generic distributions, whereas no number of pricing queries bounded in n, m, and ϵ suffices, even for generic instances learnable from polynomially many samples.

detail.abstract: Modern organizations increasingly deploy individualized work arrangements to attract and accommodate diverse talent. However, the institutional mechanisms governing workplace flexibility remain split across two distinct systems: discretionary idiosyncratic deals (i-deals) and statutory disability accommodations. Although employees across both pathways often request functionally identical structural adjustments-such as schedule flexibility and remote work-the career and psychological outcomes of these requests diverge sharply. Integrating Relational Inequality Theory (RIT) with the Social Relational Model of Disability and Conservation of Resources theory, this paper analyzes this divergence through the lens of neurodivergent employees, who face heightened barriers when navigating both systems. We delineate four foundational asymmetries governing individualized claims-making: Access (relational capital versus structural vulnerability), Meaning (value versus deficit signaling), Perception (managerial autonomy versus compliance reactance), and Identity (cognitive masking versus medicalized disclosure). Furthermore, we show how both individualized pathways provoke lateral coworker backlash due to perceived favoritism and medical information asymmetry. To overcome these structural inequalities, we argue that organizations must move away from individual bargaining and adopt "collective flexibility"-operationalizing universal design in HR policy to institutionalize variation and dismantle flexibility stigma.

Examining major projects—including the Port of Chancay, the Bioceanic Railway, and urban toll Public-Private Partnerships (Rutas de Lima and Línea Amarilla)—the study highlights the structural mismatch between Peru's exceptional geographic fortune and its chronic institutional weakness. detail.abstract: Decision-making is a crucial aspect of management, as it plays a vital role in achieving organizational goals effectively and efficiently. This paper examines managerial levels and types of organizational decisions, including strategic, tactical, operational, programmed, and non-programmed decisions. The study employs a literature review methodology, analyzing relevant sources regarding management and decision-making. The findings indicate that each managerial level possesses distinct characteristics and responsibilities within the decisionmaking process. Strategic decisions are formulated by top-level management to determine the organization's long-term direction and sustainability, whereas tactical decisions focus on achieving short-to medium-term goals by weighing various alternatives, costs, benefits, and qualitative factors. Operational decisions pertain to the execution of daily activities, supervision, target achievement, and the efficient use of resources. Regarding the nature of the issues involved, programmed decisions are applied to routine situations governed by clear procedures or rules, while non-programmed decisions address unique, non-routine problems requiring creativity, analysis, and critical thinking. Consequently, selecting the appropriate type of decision based on managerial level and the nature of the issue enables organizations to conduct their activities in a more focused, effective, and efficient manner.

detail.abstract: Individuals are often reluctant to follow machine learning-powered recommendations. To address this, explanations of the logic underlying these recommendations have been proposed as a means of increasing adoption. However, it is not well understood whether the effectiveness of explanations depends on who is affected by a user's decision-the user or a third party. This question is particularly relevant in contexts such as healthcare, financial, and public-sector decision-making, where decisionmakers frequently use algorithmic recommendations to make consequential decisions for others. We examine these questions using a controlled incentivized experiment with a context-neutral prediction task in which participants make repeated adoption decisions. We manipulate whether (i) a participant receives an explanation of the logic underlying the algorithmic recommendation and (ii) the affected party is the participant (Self treatment) or a matched individual (Other treatment). We find that, in the absence of explanations, adoption of algorithmic recommendations is similar regardless of the affected party. We also observe that explanations significantly increase adoption in Self, but have no discernible effect in Other, identifying the affected party as an important boundary condition for their effectiveness. Moreover, in Self, explanations attenuate the decline in adoption associated with unfavorable experiences with model errors; we do not observe this buffering effect in Other. Our findings thus show that explanations can shape how reliance on AI evolves with the user's experience (model performance), but their effectiveness does not extend uniformly across decision contexts. For organizations deploying AI-enabled decision support, explanations should therefore not be viewed as a one-size-fits-all intervention for supporting appropriate reliance.

detail.abstract: Background: Research on child sexual abuse (CSA) has generated substantial knowledge about trauma reactions and disclosure experiences, but large-scale quantitative studies typically rely on predefined constructs, whereas qualitative studies preserve survivors’ own words and contextual complexity but are difficult to apply systematically across large samples. Open-ended survey responses may bridge these approaches if organized systematically.Objective: To develop and refine a coding framework for systematic analysis of free-text descriptions of reactions to CSA and perceived social responses to disclosure. Participants and Setting: The framework was developed from four open-ended questions in an intake assessment battery completed in three regional Danish treatment centers by 1,398 sexually abused treatment-seeking adults (mean age = 36.7 years, SD = 12.0, range 18–79). Among participants with available gender data, 85.9% were women and 14.0% were men.Methods: Using a codebook-oriented thematic analysis approach, the framework was developed abductively through iterative phases combining empirical coding, theory, coder discussions, and inter-rater reliability testing. Cohen’s kappa was used to guide refinement rather than as a fixed criterion of coding quality.Results: The final framework comprised a CSA-reaction component with six categories: dissociation, emotions, thoughts, behavior, bodily and cognitive reactions and sequelae, and memory. The disclosure component included two macro-level dimensions – overall response and subsequent action or inaction – and non-mutually exclusive micro-codes mainly capturing specific confidant reactions.Conclusions: The framework provides a structured but flexible approach for transforming survivors’ own descriptions into analyzable data while maintaining attention to contextual meaning during coding.

detail.title: Association of Diagnostic Labels With Anxiety and Treatment Decisions in Low-Risk Thyroid Cancer: A Randomized Crossover Experiment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract:
Background: Overdiagnosis and potential overtreatment of low-risk thyroid cancer are growing concerns in China. Diagnostic labels can influence anxiety and treatment preferences, but whether these effects generalize to Chinese populations and remain consistent across sequential label exposures is uncertain.

Methods: We conducted a randomized crossover online survey among 644 Chinese adults between October and December 2024. Participants were presented, in random order, with three diagnostic labels describing the same low-risk thyroid cancer scenario (“thyroid cancer,” “thyroid tumor,” and “thyroid nodule”). For each label, participants rated diagnostic anxiety (0–10 scale) and selected a treatment option (total thyroidectomy, partial thyroidectomy, or active surveillance), followed by rating treatment-related anxiety. Differences across labels and presentation sequences were analyzed using analysis of variance and mixed-effects models. An exploratory scenario analysis estimated potential differences in annual thyroidectomy expenditure in China.

Results: Diagnostic anxiety differed across labels (P < 0.05), with the highest mean score for “thyroid cancer” (6.55) and the lowest for “thyroid nodule” (4.55). Active surveillance was most frequently selected under the “thyroid nodule” label (64.60%), compared with 40.84% under the “thyroid cancer” label. Under the “thyroid cancer” label, 26.71% selected total thyroidectomy and 32.45% selected partial thyroidectomy.Later exposure to the “thyroid cancer” label was associated with higher anxiety and increased likelihood of selecting surgery. Model-based estimates suggested that replacing “cancer” with “tumor” or “nodule” could reduce annual costs by approximately $96.50 million and $196.74 million, respectively.

Conclusions: Among Chinese adults responding to hypothetical scenarios, diagnostic labels elicited different levels of anxiety and management preferences. Labels that conveyed cancer were associated with a greater preference for surgical management, suggesting that diagnostic communication could influence decisions in preference-sensitive settings. Whether these effects translate into actual treatment uptake or potentially avoidable surgery requires evaluation among patients facing real clinical decisions.

title: Anti-Recharacterization Laws and Labor Investment Efficiency
affiliations: Ozyegin University

detail.title: Anti-Recharacterization Laws and Labor Investment Efficiency

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the effect of relaxing financing constraints on firms' labor investment efficiency. Using the staggered adoption of anti-recharacterization laws (ARLs) in U.S. states as an exogenous shock that relaxed firms' financing constraints, I find that labor investment efficiency improves significantly following ARL adoption. The improvement is concentrated in underemployment, with no statistically significant effect on overemployment. The effect is stronger among financially constrained firms and firms in industries with higher labor adjustment costs. A dynamic analysis finds no statistically significant pre-adoption trend. These findings provide causal evidence that relaxing financing constraints improves firms' labor investment efficiency.

detail.abstract: In contemporary fractured institutional environments, corporations are routinely forced to engage with polarizing sociopolitical and cultural issues. While prior literature has predominantly examined corporate sociopolitical activism (CSA) and CEO activism as episodic communicative events or public relations crises, this study establishes an organizational-level framework that conceptualizes sociopolitical engagement as an enduring strategic posture. Grounded in Resource Dependence Theory (RDT), institutional decoupling, and typological logic, we introduce a two-dimensional framework of Corporate Sociopolitical Positioning (CSP) defined by Identity Coherence (longitudinal normative consistency) and Substantive Commitment (material resource and governance allocation). Crossing these dimensions yields four distinct strategic archetypes: Integrated Advocates, Performative Signalers, Situational Responders, and Opportunistic Reactors. We examine the distinct strategic trade-offs, stakeholder counterpositioning dynamics, and vulnerability profiles characteristic of each archetype. Furthermore, we outline critical boundary conditions governing the strategic viability of these postures, focusing on market structures (B2B vs. B2C) and the institutional tolerance of the operating environment, illustrated through corporate responses in emerging markets. The paper concludes by tracing the dynamic, non-linear trajectories through which firms transition across configurations over time.

title: Comparative Analysis of Control Algorithms for Continuous Glucose Monitoring Systems: A Simulation Study
affiliations: University of Louisiana at Lafayette - University of Louisiana at Lafayette, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Arkansas at Little Rock

detail.title: Comparative Analysis of Control Algorithms for Continuous Glucose Monitoring Systems: A Simulation Study

affiliations.org_name: University of Louisiana at Lafayette - University of Louisiana at Lafayette

detail.abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring systems are integral to the management of Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus providing real-time blood glucose readings and enabling insulin regulation. This study evaluates various control strategies for automated insulin delivery systems, including the classic Bergman Minimal Model, a standard Proportional Integral-Derivative (PID) controller, a modified PID controller incorporating physiological insights, zone-based Model Predictive Control (MPC), a modified zone-MPC with enhanced stability features, and a reinforcement learning (RL) based approach. Using synthetic glucose datasets for training and testing, we simulated the performance of these algorithms based on critical metrics such as Time in Range (TIR), mean glucose levels, insulin usage, and glycemic variability (GV). The results demonstrate distinct trade-offs between control paradigms. The RL controller achieved the optimal clinical 1balance, yielding the highest TIR (89.02% ± 5.62%) and lowest GV (18.04% ± 4.16%) with zero Time Below Range, while utilizing highly physiological insulin totals ( 98 U/day). In contrast, model-based controllers (PID and Zone-MPC) required slightly higher insulin delivery ( 91–150 U/day) to manage synthetic meal disturbances, highlighting the unique adaptability and insulin efficiency of data-driven approaches in automated insulin delivery. This study highlights the trade-offs between adaptability, performance, and implementation parameters in the development of automated insulin delivery systems.

detail.abstract:
Background: Menopausal symptoms vary widely in number and perceived impact, but it is unclear whether these dimensions are differently associated with healthcare-seeking and menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) use. We examined the independent associations of symptom count and perceived impact on well-being with healthcare-seeking and MHT use among people reporting perimenopause or menopause-related symptoms.

Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of an online survey of adults aged 18-75 years who had experienced perimenopause or menopause-related symptoms. Symptom count was calculated from ten prespecified symptoms, and perceived impact on overall well-being was rated from no to severe impact. Healthcare-seeking was defined as having sought medical advice for symptoms. Respondents who reported having tried hormone therapy were classified as having ever used MHT. Multivariable logistic regression models examined independent associations of symptom count and perceived impact with healthcare-seeking and MHT use, adjusting for age group.

Findings: Of 13 136 respondents, 12 458 (94·8%) answered yes to having experienced perimenopause or menopause-related symptoms and were included in the analysis. Participants reported a median of 8 symptoms (IQR 6–9), and 8156 (67·1%) reported a significant or severe impact on well-being. Overall, 8523 (68·4%) participants sought medical advice and 4083 (32·8%) reported having tried hormone therapy. In complete-case analyses (n=12 148), each one-category increase in perceived impact was associated with higher odds of healthcare-seeking ([aOR] 2·53, 95% CI 2·39–2·67; p<0·001), whereas symptom count was not (aOR 1·00 per additional symptom, 0·98–1·02; p=0·824). Conversely, each additional symptom was associated with higher odds of MHT use (aOR 1·21, 1·19–1·24; p<0·001), whereas perceived impact was not (aOR 0·96 per one-category increase, 0·92–1·01; p=0·112).

Interpretation: Perceived impact on well-being and symptom count were differently associated with healthcare-seeking and MHT use. Assessing how symptoms affect well-being alongside symptom number could provide a more clinically informative understanding of individuals' needs and support individualised, patient-centred menopause care.

title: Medical School Quotas And Health System Performance In South Korea: An OECD Comparative Analysis Using Frequentist And Bayesian Inference
affiliations: Hallym University and Oh Medicine and Methodology Research Institute

detail.title: Medical School Quotas And Health System Performance In South Korea: An OECD Comparative Analysis Using Frequentist And Bayesian Inference

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest regarding the publication of this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

affiliations.org_name: Oh Medicine and Methodology Research Institute

detail.abstract:
Background: In South Korea, prolonged debates over medical school quotas have intensified the need for an evidence-based assessment of physician workforce policies. In this regard, we aimed to evaluate the current position and performance based on Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) health system indicators within the context of 3,058 medical school quotas.

Methods: A cross-national meta-analysis comparing differences among various countries was conducted using four representative OECD health indicators—life expectancy, avoidable mortality, physicians’ consultations per person, and health expenditure per capita—in relation to medical school quotas. Subsequently, the OECD health indicators were categorized into five major sections: health status (total mortality), healthcare resources, healthcare utilization, health expenditure/risk factor, and health quality; the average values for South Korea were then compared with the OECD average. Furthermore, we validated the results through cross-inference (frequentist + Bayesian).

Findings: With 3,058 medical school quotas, three representative OECD health indicators, except for health expenditure, were in significantly better positions among OECD countries (life expectancy [SMD = 0.80, P < 0.001], avoidable mortality [SMD = −7.46, P < 0.001], doctor consultations per person [SMD = 20.24, P < 0.001], health expenditure per capita [SMD = −0.18, P > 0.05]). When comparing South Korea’s average with the OECD average, South Korea had better figures in all five sections, with the 3,058 medical school quotas (health status (total mortality) [SMD= −5.28, P < 0.180], healthcare resources [SMD = 6.39, P < 0.05], healthcare utilization [SMD= 10.92, P < 0.001], health expenditure/risk factor [SMD= −2.17, P > 0.05], health quality [SMD= −2.47, P > 0.05]), with significantly better figures in healthcare resources and utilization. The cross-inference analysis results indicated a trend similar to that of the meta-analysis; however, there were differences in certain aspects of confidence and credible intervals.

Interpretation: From a health system performance perspective, South Korea demonstrates robust healthcare standards despite maintaining a medical school quota of 3,058. Despite maintaining this medical school quota for two decades, South Korea's physician count and density doubled, yet essential and regional care shortages worsened. This shows workforce policy must target distribution and structure, not just overall numbers. As a hypothesis-generating policy framework, we propose a public-mission medical licensure system for future institutional evaluation.

detail.abstract:
Background: Although perinatal mortality has declined in India, evidence on how its determinants have changed over time is limited. We examined trends in perinatal mortality, stillbirth, and early neonatal mortality over four decades, and temporal changes in risk factors for perinatal mortality.

Methods: We used data from an open community-based pregnancy cohort in rural South India, including 88,774 births from 1986 to 2025. Trends were assessed using Joinpoint regression. Multivariable logistic regression identified associated factors using a pooled model adjusted for calendar year and separate decade-specific models. We assessed temporal changes in associations using decade-by-risk-factor interactions and likelihood ratio tests.

Findings: Perinatal mortality rate [PMR] declined from 55·0 to 8·9 per 1,000 total births between 1986 and 2025. Stillbirth rate declined from 29·2 to 6·0 per 1,000 total births, while early neonatal mortality rate declined from 26·6 to 3·0 per 1,000 live births. The decline in PMR accelerated after 2009, with an annual change of −2·09% (95% CI −2·99 to −0·90) during 1986–2009 and −7·48% (−12·87 to −5·48) during 2009–2025. In adjusted analyses, preterm birth was the strongest risk factor (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]: 7·07, 95% CI: 6·48–7·71), followed by previous perinatal death (2·45, 2·09–2·86), pregnancy-induced hypertension (2·12, 1·65–2·70), fewer than four antenatal care (ANC) visits (1·54, 1·41–1·68), nulliparity (1·44, 1·30–1·58), multiple gestation (1·78, 1·47–2·15), maternal height <145 cm (1·30, 1·08–1·55) and post term birth (1.22, 1.00–1.48). The association with preterm birth strengthened over time, from an aOR of 5·91 (5·12–6·82) in 1986–1995 to 15·94 (11·87–21·52) in 2016–2025. Associations with nulliparity and fewer than four ANC visits persisted, while other factors declined.

Interpretation: Perinatal mortality declined over four decades. Further progress requires better prevention and management of preterm birth and continued improvement in antenatal care.Funding: None

title: Youth perspectives on state protection and individual autonomy: A cross-country analysis

affiliations.org_name: Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN
Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN
Unaffiliated Authors - affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: Across the world, nations have established child protection systems to secure children’s safety, but there is wide variation in the circumstances that require a state response and in adult attitudes about appropriate government actions. Little is known about youth views concerning government involvement in family life. This study examines the attitudes of youth (ages 15-17) toward efforts to constrain youth high-risk behaviors, including an experimental survey design with representative samples of youth (n=2,010) from four countries (Finland, Ireland, Norway, and the U.S.). The study asks whom they believe should bear responsibility for the child’s welfare (the state, parents or youth), if the level of risk, and respondents’ rights-orientation have an impact on youth attitudes, and if there are differences between countries. The study shows that the level of risk does not yield results, but that youth view risk-behaviors as concerning and generally favor state protective supports. Rights-orientation is the most consistent driver, and country differences are most relevant for the youth autonomy dimension; female youth accord more responsibility to parents and less to the state. A takeaway for policy makers is that youth understand the need for a state response and the limitations of parental interventions in some situations.

title: When Adverse Evidence Can Count Governing Claims and the Limits of Political Accountability
affiliations: Bogazici University

detail.title: When Adverse Evidence Can Count Governing Claims and the Limits of Political Accountability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no financial support for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.

detail.abstract: Political accountability can expose officials to questioning and sanctions while leaving the claims used to justify their decisions protected from adverse assessment. This article offers a framework for identifying that selective protection. It separates evaluability, the admissibility of relevant adverse evidence against a specified governing claim, from acknowledgement by the responsible actor and enforceability through an authorised forum. Holding these apart shows that the familiar signs of accountability can attach to one object while another escapes judgment: an inquiry can sanction implementation while its terms of reference reserve the strategy that authorised it. Drawing on work on accountability, commissions of inquiry, and blame avoidance, the article identifies ideological defeat immunity as one mechanism of protection and sets out an evidentiary protocol for diagnosing exclusion. Documents on Iran's 2015 nuclear authorisation and a 2022 UK High Court climate judgment show the protocol disciplining inference in both directions. The article concludes with a limited principle of public justification: empirical claims used to support the exercise of authority must remain open to relevant adverse assessment, even when other reasons justify continued commitment.

title: Another Moment for CAPM
affiliations: Emory University - Department of Finance

detail.title: Another Moment for CAPM

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: The non-Gaussian CAPM states that beta and coskewness are the only two systematic risks: beta captures second-order risk, while coskewness captures third-order risk. However, the empirical performance of coskewness is known to be weak. Using a return-moment expansion, I decompose coskewness into a sum of correlations between stock and market moments. If investors care less about higher-order risks, these components should receive unequal prices. In Fama-MacBeth regressions of individual stocks excluding microcaps, only the lowest-order component, the variance-variance correlation, earns a significant premium; higher-order cross-moment correlations do not. Thus, third-order risk is priced, but in a more nuanced way. A strategy combining beta and the variance-variance correlation earns about 9% annually, unexplained by Fama-French factors.

title: Deterministic Equal Sanctions under Shared Sanction Capacity: Strict Dominance, Unique Pure Nash, and a Mixed-Strategy Boundary
affiliations: Independent researcher

detail.title: Deterministic Equal Sanctions under Shared Sanction Capacity: Strict Dominance, Unique Pure Nash, and a Mixed-Strategy Boundary

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: How does an enforcement-capacity problem change when the implementation objective is weakened while the enforcement technology is fixed? I study a one-shot binary-action game with static, deterministic, count-based equal sanctions subject to shared capacity. Under strict-dominance implementation, feasibility is monotone and the full-capacity rule yields a sharp closed-form threshold. The principal result concerns the weaker objective that all-C be the unique pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. Bad profiles can then be eliminated either by insider exit or outsider entry. This disjunctive structure couples adjacent cardinality layers and makes feasibility nonmonotone in sanction coordinates: raising a sanction can restore a bad equilibrium by deterring outsider entry. A backward equilibrium-elimination recursion gives a necessary-and-sufficient capacity characterization. Finally, unique pure-strategy implementation coincides with full Nash uniqueness for two agents under a strict all-C entrance condition, but robustly separates from it with three agents.

detail.abstract: We quantify the effects of uncertainty about the conduct of monetary policy on asset prices. Nominal yields, real yields, stock returns, and implied volatilities all vary more on days with FOMC communication than on FOMC “blackout” days, consistent with policy communication being a source of risk. Furthermore, these asset prices all respond significantly to changes in interest-rate uncertainty around FOMC announcements, consistent with that risk being priced. A New Keynesian model with stochastic variation in the policy rule quantitatively matches this evidence. Our model shows that monetary-policy risk contributes to excess returns on equities and nominal bonds and accounts for much of the risk premium on inflation-indexed bonds. Transitory increases in monetary-policy risk lower stock and bond prices, reduce inflation-risk premia, and generate macroeconomic weakness similar to that produced by aggregate-demand shocks. The effective lower bound on interest rates reduces the size of monetary-policy risk in the model but magnifies its asset-pricing consequences, consistent with the data. We use our model to assess the effects of the increase in monetary-policy risk that occurred following the rapid tightening of policy in 2022.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces a geometric framework that decomposes the quality of time-series
momentum signals through the lens of information geometry. We embed the distribu-
tional dynamics of each asset into a statistical manifold endowed with the Fisher-Rao
metric, and extract a coordinate-free diagnostic-directional purity (Φ), that isolates the
fraction of distributional movement attributable to location shifts rather than scale dis-
tortions. We show that weighting momentum positions by Φα (α > 0) yields a strat-
egy we call Information-Geometric Momentum (IGM), which delivers an out-of-sample
Sharpe ratio of 0.847 across 17 ETFs spanning four asset classes (2014-2025), compared
with 0.614 for the standard time-series momentum benchmark. Strikingly, the IGM and
Kalman-filter TSMOM portfolios converge statistically (p = 0.743 on a paired return dif-
ferential test), suggesting that both the geometric and state-space approaches detect the
same latent signal. A certainty-equivalent return analysis segments the investor universe:
standard TSMOM dominates for low risk aversion (γ ≤ 2), IGM for institutional risk
preferences (γ = 3-10), and Kalman-filter TSMOM for the most risk-averse allocators
(γ ≥ 15). We establish boundary conditions by demonstrating that the Φ diagnostic
loses predictive power on futures markets, where roll-yield contamination attenuates the
relationship between directional purity and forward returns. The framework contributes
a new lens through which practitioners can evaluate when and why momentum signals
carry information, rather than merely whether they do.

title: The Problem of Rulemaking in Uncertain Patent Markets
affiliations: George Mason University - Interdisciplinary Center for Economic Science

detail.title: The Problem of Rulemaking in Uncertain Patent Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: Grant from Vetenskapsrådet

affiliations.org_name: George Mason University - Department of Economics

detail.abstract:
This article discusses the sociological implications of irreducible ex-ante uncertainty in patent markets. One can break down the firms' management of uncertainty in two sequential steps and characterize the first step as a sociological process where firms must define the rules of the game within which in the second step, economically efficient exchange can take place. Firms cannot explicitly coordinate/collude but can use patenting strategies (investing in patent assets) as a device to signal and coordinate on the rules of the game. Through qualitative interviews I identify the types of signaling strategies and the conditions of exchange that derive from those. 

Four types of strategies were discovered – staying clear – strategic alignment – marginal transactions – systemic abuse – which all result in mutually assured self-restraint not to sue nor harm.

title: Systemic Liquidity Insulation in High-Velocity Digital Payment Networks: An Asymmetric Macro-Financial Circuit Breaker Framework
affiliations: Addis Ababa University, School of Commerce and Addis Ababa University

detail.title: Systemic Liquidity Insulation in High-Velocity Digital Payment Networks: An Asymmetric Macro-Financial Circuit Breaker Framework

affiliations.org_name: Addis Ababa University, School of Commerce

detail.abstract: The global transition toward Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) and instant digital payment rails has fundamentally altered the physics of systemic financial risk. In emerging economies, the collapse of legacy batch-clearing latency windows has introduced the threat of high-velocity ”digital bank runs,” where localized capital flight at peripheral microfinance institutions can instantaneously drain macro-structural central banking liquidity pools. This paper introduces a novel econometric policy instrument—the Asymmetric Macro-Financial Circuit Breaker—designed to mitigate systemic contagion without halting organic market operations. By mathematically decoupling micro-operational transaction velocities (v(t)) from primary macro-structural capital vaults (Λ(T)), the framework establishes a Dynamic Liquidity Settlement Threshold (λ(t)). Under conditions of acute volumetric stress, the architecture activates an asymmetric camouflage state, buffering anomalous capital flight at the network edge. Empirical macro-simulations demonstrate that under a 3,000% liquidity shock, legacy RTGS systems suffer catastrophic contagion, whereas the proposed asymmetric shield drives the systemic spillover coefficient (Rspill) asymptotically to zero, perfectly insulating the sovereign capital vault. This framework provides central banking authorities with a decentralized, non-invasive mechanism to safely liberalize retail payment networks while enforcing strict macro-prudential stability.

detail.abstract: Mesoporous carbons combine high surface area, tunable pore architecture, chemical robustness, and adjustable surface chemistry, which makes them attractive supports for transition metal nanoparticles in heterogeneous catalysis. Since the introduction of ordered mesoporous carbons by nanocasting, research has expanded to soft-templating routes, heteroatom doping, and confinement strategies that aim to control particle size, location, and stability. This review synthesizes peer-reviewed literature on the synthesis of mesoporous carbon supports, methods for introducing transition metals, and the structural features that govern catalytic performance. It then identifies unresolved problems: limited control over where particles reside, incomplete understanding of metal-support interactions in carbon, inconsistent testing of leaching and recyclability, and weak comparability between studies. Building on these observations, the paper proposes a conceptual design-validation framework linking support architecture, metal confinement, multifunctionality, and standardized evaluation. The framework is a synthesis intended for empirical testing and has not been experimentally validated here. The review concludes that progress depends less on new material variants than on rigorous, comparable characterization of active-site location, transport effects, and long-term stability. Practical implications for catalyst developers and research directions for the field are outlined.

title: Chirality as Broken Put–Call Symmetry
affiliations: ETH Zurich, MYRA School of Business and MIT

detail.title: Chirality as Broken Put–Call Symmetry

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

affiliations.org_name: Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich (ETH Zurich)

detail.abstract:
We define financial chirality directly from option prices as the violation of put–call symmetry (PCS) about the forward. PCS is the option market’s native mirror: under it a call struck at X is worth X/F puts struck at F2/X, and the mirror is fixed by no-arbitrage rather than chosen.[1] Building on the characterisation of Carr and Lee (2009), under which PCS is equivalent to evenness of the tilted density ex/2f(x) of the log-return, to symmetry of the cumulant generating function ψ about ½ and to an even smile, we develop three complementary measures of its violation: a strike-by-strike chirality function χPCS(k), which normalises the skewness premium of Bates (1991) into an exactly odd function and is the price of a static mirror spread; a bounded magnitude, the chirality concentration measure (CCM); and a signed handedness η = −ψ′(½), which equals the Hellinger skew of Schneider and Trojani (2019) normalised by the half-share mass. To leading order η ≈ κ3/24 + κ4/48, so chirality is not skewness: markets with skewness of about −0.11 can be exactly achiral, and achirality predicts a neutral skewness of about −½κσ. Delta-hedging the strip that replicates the numerator of η yields a continuous-monitoring counterpart of their Hellinger skew swap, whose floating leg is realised variance weighted by an odd function of the running log-return.

On daily S&P 500 options from 2010 to 2015, the mirror spread lies outside the conservative bid–ask bounds on essentially every day at every strike and maturity, and handedness is negative on more than 99.8% of days. The cumulant expansion holds on market-implied moments, with the fourth-cumulant term offsetting a median 12% of the third-cumulant term at one month, a component that skewness-based measures omit. The pathwise swap identity holds on actual index paths (correlation 0.999 between the floating leg and the hedged-strip P&L), realised handedness averages 17% of implied, and the implied–realised chirality spread is negative (−0.09 bp per month, t = −4.4). The spread rejects pure variance scaling, and after an ex-ante variance risk premium control the regression leaves a residual mean of −0.051 bp per month (t = −2.9); we do not interpret the residual as a separately priced factor.

detail.abstract: We apply the put-call-symmetry (PCS) definition of financial chirality to foreign exchange, where the mirror is physical. Currency inversion is a change of numeraire that maps the cumulant generating function by ψB/A(u) = ψA/B(1-u); it implies a model-independent reciprocal-pair price identity, a smile-mirror identity under Garman-Kohlhagen quoting, and a parity theorem under which the handedness η, the chirality function and the smile-based index change sign while the chirality concentration measure is unchanged. Delta-space quotes are centred at the delta-neutral straddle strike kDNS, not at the forward where the PCS mirror sits. For a stylized quadratic smile under forward, premium-unadjusted deltas the chirality-neutral risk reversal is (2/Φ-1 (0.75))•Σ25-SS•ΣATM√T ≈ 2.965•Σ25-SS•ΣATM√T, and the three-quote estimator of the smile-based index is recentred at the forward as χ̂FX,25-kDNS, with kDNS = ±½ΣATM 2 T according to the premium convention. On published one-month quotes the recentred estimator matches the exact three-point index to within 0.3% for premium-unadjusted EURUSD, while for premium-adjusted USDJPY the asymmetry of the 25-delta strikes dominates and the actual strikes must be used. Reconstructing FX-style quotes from about 1,500 daily S&P 500 smiles, where dense strikes supply exact benchmarks, confirms that three conventional quotes identify the sign of handedness on more than 99.8% of days and its ranking closely (rank correlations of 0.92 and 0.95 at one and three months), but not its absolute level. We show that the reciprocal-pair identities hold by construction on consistently quoted surfaces and are therefore consistency checks, and we set out the panel tests that are informative.
